1V1.1

sc-Banach spaces, sums and shifts

restated

to confirmAn sc-Banach space is a sequence of Banach spaces $E_0 \supset E_1 \supset \cdots$ with compact inclusions and $E_\infty$ dense in every $E_m$, taken as an indexed family with injective compact inclusions; finite-dimensional spaces carry the constant structure, sums have levels $E_m \oplus F_m$, and $E^k$ has levels $E_{k+m}$.

indexed family, not nested subspacesinjectivity of the inclusions a fieldonly one structure in finite dim. (V1.31)
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §1.1, Definition 1.1, p. 6

An sc-structure on a Banach space $E$ is a decreasing sequence of Banach spaces $E = E_0 \supset E_1 \supset E_2 \supset \cdots$ such that (1) every inclusion $E_{m+1} \to E_m$ is compact and (2) $E_\infty = \bigcap_m E_m$ is dense in every $E_m$. A Banach space with an sc-structure is an sc-Banach space; points of $E_\infty$ are smooth, points of $E_m$ have regularity $m$. A finite-dimensional space has exactly one sc-structure, the constant one. A subset $A$ inherits the filtration $A_m = A \cap E_m$, and $A^k$ is $A_k$ with the filtration $(A^k)_m = A_{k+m}$. The direct sum $E \oplus F$ has levels $E_m \oplus F_m$.

Example 1.2, the weighted Sobolev spaces $H^{m,\delta_m}(\mathbb R \times S^1)$, is not formalized (G.1).

Verified edition V1.1

A scale consists of real Banach spaces $E_m$, $m \in \mathbb N$, and injective compact continuous linear maps $E_{m+1} \to E_m$; $\iota_m : E_m \to E_0$ is the composite, $E_\infty \subseteq E_0$ the subspace of points that lie in $\iota_m(E_m)$ for every $m$, and $E_\infty \cap E_m := \iota_m^{-1}(E_\infty)$. An sc-Banach space is a scale in which $E_\infty \cap E_m$ is dense in $E_m$ for every $m$. Consequences: the image of $E_{m+k}$ in $E_m$ is dense. Constructions: for a finite-dimensional normed space $V$ the constant family $E_m = V$, with identity inclusions, is an sc-Banach space all of whose points are smooth; for sc-Banach spaces $E$, $F$, the family $E_m \times F_m$ with the product inclusions is an sc-Banach space $E \oplus F$ whose smooth points at level $m$ are the pairs of smooth points; the family $E_{m+1}$ with the inclusions of $E$ is an sc-Banach space $E^1$ whose smooth points at level $m$ are those of $E$ at level $m + 1$; $E^k$ is the $k$-fold iterate. For $U \subseteq E_0$, the level set $U_m := \iota_m^{-1}(U) \subseteq E_m$. Book: Definition 1.1, p. 6: a decreasing sequence of Banach spaces $E = E_0 \supset E_1 \supset \cdots$ with compact inclusions and $E_\infty = \bigcap E_m$ dense in every $E_m$; the constant structure on a finite-dimensional space; $(E \oplus F)_m = E_m \oplus F_m$; the filtration $A_m = A \cap E_m$ of a subset and the shift $A^k$. Hidden hypotheses: the inclusions are injective (implicit in "$\subset$") and continuous (part of compactness). Deviation (restated): the $E_m$ are separate Banach spaces, not subsets of one space; the two pictures are equivalent and nothing in Chapter 1 uses more than the family. The text's remarks that a finite-dimensional space has only the constant structure and that the constant family on an infinite-dimensional space is not an sc-structure are V1.31.

What differs (the comparison)

  • The text's $E_m$ are subsets of one space $E$; the formal scale is a family of separate Banach spaces with injective compact inclusions, and "$x \in E_m$" for $x \in E_0$ means $x \in \iota_m(E_m)$. The two pictures are equivalent, and nothing in Chapter 1 uses more than the family.
  • Injectivity of the inclusions, implicit in "$E_{m+1} \subset E_m$", is a field of the structure; continuity is part of being a compact operator in Mathlib's sense.
  • Condition (2) is taken exactly as stated, density of $E_\infty \cap E_m$ in every $E_m$. The weaker "$E_{m+1}$ is dense in $E_m$" is derived, not assumed.
  • That a finite-dimensional space has only the constant structure, and that the constant sequence on an infinite-dimensional space is not an sc-structure, are proved separately (V1.31).
2V1.2

sc-operators and sc-isomorphisms

restated

to confirmAn sc-operator is a linear map continuous $E_m \to F_m$ on every level, given by its level maps; an sc-isomorphism is one that is a continuous linear equivalence on every level.

the level maps are the dataIsScOperator is the text's formcontinuity on the levels is automatic
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §1.1, Definition 1.3, p. 7

A linear map $T : E \to F$ between sc-Banach spaces is an sc-operator if $T(E_m) \subset F_m$ and the induced $T : E_m \to F_m$ is continuous for every $m$. A linear sc-isomorphism is a bijective sc-operator whose inverse is an sc-operator.

Verified edition V1.2

An sc-operator $T : E \to F$ between sc-Banach spaces is a family of continuous linear maps $T_m : E_m \to F_m$ with $\iota^F_m T_{m+1} = T_m \iota^E_m$; the family is determined by $T_0$, and a continuous linear $T_0 : E_0 \to F_0$ is an sc-operator exactly when for each $m$ some continuous linear $T_m : E_m \to F_m$ satisfies $\iota_m T_m = T_0 \iota_m$ (the two formulations correspond). Sc-operators compose, add, and map smooth points to smooth points. An sc-isomorphism is a family of continuous linear equivalences $E_m \simeq F_m$ commuting with the inclusions; inverses and composites are sc-isomorphisms. A continuous linear $T_0 : E_0 \to F_0$ with $T_0(E_m) \subseteq F_m$ for every $m$ is an sc-operator (the continuity of $T_0 : E_m \to F_m$ is the closed graph theorem), and an sc-operator bijective on every level is an sc-isomorphism (the open mapping theorem). Book: Definition 1.3, p. 7. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): the level maps are data, with the text's predicate on the base map recovered as Polyfold.IsScOperator; the continuity of the inverse of a bijective sc-operator on each level, which the text's definition of an sc-isomorphism demands, is built into the formal notion, and derived from the open mapping theorem separately (Polyfold.ScIso.ofBijective); the continuity on the levels asked by Definition 1.3 is automatic for a bounded $T_0$ that maps $E_m$ into $F_m$ (Findings, Chapter 3, item 233).

What differs (the comparison)

  • In the family picture an sc-operator carries its level maps as data; the text's "one linear map $T$ mapping $E_m$ into $F_m$ continuously" is the predicate IsScOperator on the base map, and the two are interchangeable (ScOperator.isScOperator, IsScOperator.toScOperator).
  • An sc-isomorphism is given by level-wise continuous linear equivalences; that the inverse of a bijective sc-operator is continuous on each level (the open mapping theorem) is built into this definition, and proved separately (ScIso.ofBijective). Likewise the continuity of $T : E_m \to F_m$ asked by Definition 1.3 is automatic for a bounded $T_0$ that maps $E_m$ into $F_m$ (isScOperator_of_mapsTo, the closed graph theorem; Findings, Chapter 3, item 233). sc⁺-operators

as in the book

to confirmAn sc⁺-operator is an sc-operator $E \to F^1$; it is compact $E_m \to F_m$ on every level.

the first condition is the secondsc-compactness proved
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §1.1, Definition 1.4, p. 7

An sc-operator $S : E \to F$ is an $\mathrm{sc}^+$-operator if $S(E_m) \subset F_{m+1}$ and $S : E \to F^1$ is an sc-operator. Since the inclusion $F_{m+1} \to F_m$ is compact, an $\mathrm{sc}^+$-operator is sc-compact: $S : E_m \to F_m$ is compact for every $m$.

Verified edition V1.3

An $\mathrm{sc}^+$-operator $E \to F$ is an sc-operator $E \to F^1$, i.e. continuous linear $S_m : E_m \to F_{m+1}$ commuting with the inclusions. Composed with the inclusion $F^1 \to F$ (an sc-operator) it is an sc-operator $E \to F$ whose level-$m$ map $E_m \to F_m$ is compact for every $m$, and which raises the level: $x \in \iota_m(E_m)$ implies $S_0 x \in \iota_{m+1}(F_{m+1})$. Book: Definition 1.4, p. 7, and the remark that follows it: an sc-operator $S$ with $S(E_m) \subset F_{m+1}$ and $S : E \to F^1$ an sc-operator is sc-compact. Hidden hypotheses: none; the condition $S(E_m) \subset F_{m+1}$ is contained in "$S : E \to F^1$ is an sc-operator" and is dropped.

4V1.4

sc-subspaces and sc-splittings

restated

to confirmAn sc-subspace is a closed subspace whose smooth points are dense in each $F \cap E_m$; an sc-splitting $E = F \oplus G$ consists of two sc-subspaces with $F_m$ and $G_m$ complementary on every level.

compactness of $F_{m+1} \to F_m$ automatictopological sum from IsCompl + closedness
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §1.1, Definition 1.5, p. 7

A subspace $F$ of an sc-Banach space $E$ is an sc-subspace if $F$ is closed and $F_m = F \cap E_m$ defines an sc-structure on $F$. An sc-subspace $F$ has an sc-complement if there is an algebraic complement $G$ such that $G_m = G \cap E_m$ is an sc-structure on $G$ and $E_m = F_m \oplus G_m$ is a topological direct sum on every level; $E = F \oplus G$ is then an sc-splitting.

Verified edition V1.4

For a subspace $A \subseteq E_0$ let $A_m := \iota_m^{-1}(A) \subseteq E_m$, closed if $A$ is. $A$ is an sc-subspace if $A$ is closed and $A_m$ is contained in the closure of $A_m \cap E_\infty$ for every $m$. A closed $A$ with the levels $A_m$ and the restricted inclusions is a scale (the restricted inclusions are compact), and an sc-subspace is in this way an sc-Banach space. $E = F \oplus G$ is an sc-splitting if $F$ and $G$ are sc-subspaces and $F_m$, $G_m$ are complementary subspaces of $E_m$ for every $m$; then $F_m$ is closed complemented in $E_m$, and the splitting is symmetric in $F$ and $G$. Book: Definition 1.5, p. 7: $F$ closed with $(F \cap E_m)$ an sc-structure; an sc-complement $G$ with $(G \cap E_m)$ an sc-structure and $E_m = F_m \oplus G_m$ a topological direct sum on every level. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): the closedness of $F_m$ in $E_m$ and the compactness of $F_{m+1} \to F_m$ are automatic and are not conditions; "topological direct sum" is read as complementary closed subspaces, the continuity of the projections following from the closed graph theorem (Polyfold.ScBanach.IsScSplitting.closedComplemented).

Polyfold.ScBanach.levelSubPolyfold.ScBanach.isClosed_levelSubPolyfold.ScBanach.IsScSubspacePolyfold.ScBanach.ofSubspaceScalePolyfold.ScBanach.ofSubspacePolyfold.ScBanach.IsScSplittingPolyfold.ScBanach.IsScSplitting.closedComplementedPolyfold.ScBanach.IsScSplitting.symm

What differs (the comparison)

  • Of the conditions in "$(F_m)$ is an sc-structure on $F$", the closedness of $F_m$ in $E_m$ and the compactness of $F_{m+1} \to F_m$ follow from the closedness of $F$ (restriction of a compact operator), so IsScSubspace asks only for closedness and the density of $F \cap E_\infty$ in each $F_m$; the sc-Banach space $F$ is then built (ScBanach.ofSubspace).
  • "Topological direct sum $E_m = F_m \oplus G_m$" is read as: $F_m$ and $G_m$ are complementary closed subspaces of $E_m$; by the closed graph theorem the sum is then topological, which is recorded as a consequence (IsScSplitting.closedComplemented). The text's "$G$ an algebraic complement with $(G_m)$ an sc-structure" is the requirement that $G$ be an sc-subspace.

Proposition 1.6

as in the book

to confirmA finite-dimensional subspace is an sc-subspace iff it lies in $E_\infty$, and then has an sc-complement.

proof: a continuous projection onto $F$
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §1.1, Proposition 1.6, p. 7

A finite-dimensional subspace $F$ of an sc-Banach space $E$ is an sc-subspace if and only if $F \subset E_\infty$. A finite-dimensional sc-subspace always has an sc-complement.

Verified edition V1.5

Let $E$ be an sc-Banach space and $F \subseteq E_0$ a finite-dimensional subspace. $F$ is an sc-subspace if and only if $F \le E_\infty$; and if $F \le E_\infty$ there is a subspace $G \subseteq E_0$ such that $E = F \oplus G$ is an sc-splitting. Book: p. 7, the same. Hidden hypotheses: none. Proof: as in the text, with a continuous projection $E_0 \to F$ from Mathlib (Hahn–Banach), lifted to each level through $F_m \cong F$.

Polyfold.ScBanach.proposition_1_6_iffPolyfold.ScBanach.proposition_1_6

What differs (the comparison)

  • The proof follows the text: a continuous projection $p : E_0 \to F$ (Mathlib's closed complementation of finite-dimensional subspaces, i.e. Hahn–Banach) is lifted to each level through $F_m \cong F$, $G = \ker p$, and the density of $G \cap E_\infty$ in $G_m$ comes from $g = (1 - P_m)g$ with $P_m$ the level projection, exactly as on p. 8.

Proposition 1.7

stronger

to confirmFor a closed subspace $A$ of an sc-Banach space $E$, the quotients $E_m/A_m$ form an sc-Banach space $E/A$ with the quotient map an sc-operator whose level kernels are the $A_m$.

any closed $A$, not only sc-subspaces$(E/A)_\infty$ identified in V1.33
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §1.1, Proposition 1.7, p. 8

If $E$ is an sc-Banach space and $A \subset E$ an sc-subspace, then $E/A$ with the filtration $E_m/A_m$ is an sc-Banach space, where $E_m/A_m = \{(x + A) \cap E_m : x \in E\}$.

Verified edition V1.6

Let $E$ be an sc-Banach space and $A \subseteq E_0$ a closed subspace. The quotient Banach spaces $E_m/A_m$, with the inclusions $E_{m+1}/A_{m+1} \to E_m/A_m$ induced by $\iota$ (injective and compact), and with the smooth points dense on every level, form an sc-Banach space $E/A$, and the quotient maps $E_m \to E_m/A_m$ form an sc-operator $E \to E/A$. As a statement: there exist an sc-Banach space $Q$ and an sc-operator $q : E \to Q$ with every $q_m$ surjective and $\ker q_m = A_m$. Book: p. 8, for an sc-subspace $A$: $E/A$ with the filtration $E_m/A_m$ is an sc-Banach space, where $E_m/A_m$ is identified with $\{(x + A) \cap E_m : x \in E\}$. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (stronger): only closedness of $A$ is used, not that $A$ is an sc-subspace. The text's identification of $E_m/A_m$ with a subset of $E/A$ is the injectivity of the induced inclusion, which holds because $A_m$ is the full preimage of $A$. The text's description of $(E/A)_\infty$ as the classes of points of $E_\infty$ is V1.33; only the trivial inclusion is used here.

sc-Fredholm operators and the index

restated

to confirmAn sc-Fredholm operator is an sc-operator with sc-splittings $E = \ker T \oplus X$, $F = C \oplus \operatorname{range} T$, $\ker T$ and $C$ finite-dimensional, and $T$ bijective $X_m \to \operatorname{range}(T)_m$ on every level; its index $\dim\ker T - \dim C$ is $\dim\ker T_0 - \dim\operatorname{coker} T_0$, and each $T_m$ is Fredholm.

(3) read as bijections $X_m \to Y_m$index independent of the splittingFredholm on every level
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §1.1, Definition 1.8, p. 9

An sc-operator $T : E \to F$ is sc-Fredholm if there are sc-splittings $E = K \oplus X$ and $F = C \oplus Y$ with (1) $K = \ker T$ finite-dimensional, (2) $C$ finite-dimensional and $Y = T(E)$, (3) $T : X \to Y$ an sc-isomorphism. Then $K \subset E_\infty$, $T(X_m) = Y_m$, $E_m = K \oplus X_m$ and $F = C \oplus T(E_m)$. The index is $\operatorname{ind}(T) = \dim K - \dim C$.

Verified edition V1.7

An sc-Fredholm splitting of an sc-operator $T : E \to F$ is given by subspaces $K, X \subseteq E_0$ and $C, Y \subseteq F_0$ such that $E = K \oplus X$ and $F = C \oplus Y$ are sc-splittings, $K = \ker T_0$, $Y = \operatorname{range} T_0$, $K$ and $C$ are finite-dimensional, and for every $m$ the map $T_m$ is a bijection of $X_m$ onto $Y_m$. $T$ is sc-Fredholm if a splitting exists. The index $\dim K - \dim C$ of a splitting equals $\dim \ker T_0 - \dim(F_0/\operatorname{range} T_0)$, hence does not depend on the splitting. Moreover $K \le E_\infty$; $\ker T_m = K_m$ and $\operatorname{range} T_m = Y_m$; and every $T_m : E_m \to F_m$ is a Fredholm operator in Mathlib's sense (finite-dimensional kernel, closed range of finite codimension, strict, with closed complemented kernel). Book: Definition 1.8, p. 9, with the remarks that $K \subset E_\infty$, $T(X_m) = Y_m$, $E_m = K \oplus X_m$ and "$F = C \oplus T(E_m)$" (read $F_m$), and $\operatorname{ind}(T) = \dim K - \dim C$. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): condition (3), "$T : X \to Y$ is an sc-isomorphism", is taken as the bijectivity of $T_m : X_m \to Y_m$ for every $m$; the continuity of the inverses is automatic by the open mapping theorem on the closed subspaces $X_m$, $Y_m$. The independence of the index from the splitting and the level-wise Fredholm property are not stated in the text.

  • Condition (3), "$T : X \to Y$ is an sc-isomorphism", is taken as: $T_m$ restricts to a bijection $X_m \to Y_m$ for every $m$. The continuity of the inverses is automatic (open mapping theorem between the closed subspaces $X_m$, $Y_m$), so nothing is lost.
  • The text's "$F = C \oplus T(E_m)$" (a slip for $F_m$) is the level-$m$ part of the splitting $F = C \oplus Y$ together with $\operatorname{range} T_m = Y_m$.

Proposition 1.9

as in the book

to confirmAn sc-Fredholm operator is regularizing: $T e \in F_m$ implies $e \in E_m$; conversely, an sc-operator that is Fredholm on level $0$ and regularizing is sc-Fredholm.

the text's proofconverse: $T_0$ Fredholm and regularizing
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §1.1, Proposition 1.9, p. 9

An sc-Fredholm operator $T : E \to F$ is regularizing: if $e \in E$ and $T(e) \in F_m$, then $e \in E_m$.

Verified edition V1.8

Let $T : E \to F$ be an sc-operator with an sc-Fredholm splitting, $e \in E_0$ and $m \in \mathbb N$. If $T_0 e \in \iota_m(F_m)$ then $e \in \iota_m(E_m)$. As a property of sc-operators (Polyfold.ScOperator.IsRegularizing): every sc-Fredholm operator is regularizing. Conversely, an sc-operator $T$ with $T_0$ Fredholm that is regularizing is sc-Fredholm (V1.9); so $T$ is sc-Fredholm if and only if $T_0 : E_0 \to F_0$ is Fredholm and $T$ is regularizing. Book: p. 9, the same ("an sc-Fredholm operator is regularizing"). Hidden hypotheses: none; the step "$c = 0$" uses $C \cap Y = 0$ on level $0$, as in the text. The converse is not stated in the text; it is the tool for the text's unargued “is sc-Fredholm” for operators obtained by conjugation and restriction in Chapter 3 (V3.8, V3.46, V3.96; Findings, Chapter 3, item 233).

Proposition 1.10

as in the book

to confirmThe sum of an sc-Fredholm operator and an sc⁺-operator is sc-Fredholm.

needs a bootstrap the text omitsindex preserved: V1.30the construction as a criterion (V1.8)
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §1.1, Proposition 1.10, p. 10 (proof §1.4.1, pp. 14–15)

Let $E$ and $F$ be sc-Banach spaces. If $T : E \to F$ is sc-Fredholm and $S : E \to F$ is an $\mathrm{sc}^+$-operator, then $T + S$ is sc-Fredholm.

Verified edition V1.9

Let $E$, $F$ be sc-Banach spaces, $T : E \to F$ an sc-Fredholm operator and $S : E \to F$ an $\mathrm{sc}^+$-operator. Then $T + S$ (with $S$ read as an sc-operator $E \to F$) is sc-Fredholm. Along the way, $T + S$ is regularizing in the sense of V1.8. Book: p. 10, the same; the proof is in §1.4.1, pp. 14–15. Hidden hypotheses: none. Proof: the text's, with three additions. The opening claim that $T + S : E_m \to F_m$ is Fredholm is the classical compact-perturbation theorem, proved here since Mathlib lacks it (V1.24–V1.25). The step "$y = (T+S)e$, so by Proposition 1.9 $e \in E_m$" needs a bootstrap, since $Se$ is only one level up: $Te = y - Se \in F_1$ gives $e \in E_1$, then $Se \in F_2$, and so on $m$ times; the same bootstrap gives $K_m = K_{m+1}$. The complement $C$ is the range of a linear right inverse of $F_0 \to F_0/Y$ with values in $F_\infty$ rather than the span of a lifted basis, and condition (3) of Definition 1.8 for $T + S$, which the text does not verify, is proved as the bijectivity of $(T + S)_m : X_m \to Y_m$. The text does not assert that the index is preserved; it is, and this is V1.30. The construction uses only two properties of $T + S$, that it is Fredholm on level $0$ and regularizing; with these as hypotheses it is proved as a criterion: an sc-operator that is Fredholm on level $0$ and regularizing is sc-Fredholm, and every level map is then Fredholm of the level-$0$ index (not stated in the text).

What differs (the comparison)

  • §1.4.1 says "since $T$ is regularizing, $e \in E_m$"; the hypothesis gives only $Te = y - Se \in F_1$, so the regularizing step must be iterated $m$ times (ScPlus.regularizing_add). The same bootstrap gives $K_m = K_{m+1}$.
  • The complement $C$ is built from a linear right inverse of $F_0 \to F_0/Y$ with values in the smooth points rather than from a lifted basis; condition (3) of Definition 1.8, which the text does not verify, is proved as the bijectivity of $(T+S)_m : X_m \to Y_m$.
  • The classical fact that opens §1.4.1, a compact perturbation of a Fredholm operator is Fredholm, is not in Mathlib and is proved here (V1.25). The text does not record that the index is preserved; the formalization proves it separately (V1.30).
  • §1.4.1 uses two properties of $T + S$ only: it is Fredholm on level $0$, and it is regularizing (so its kernel lies in $E_\infty$, it maps $E_m$ onto $Y \cap F_m$, and its range has a complement spanned by smooth points). With these as hypotheses the construction is a criterion for sc-Fredholm operators (isScFredholm_of_isRegularizing), not stated in the text (Findings, Chapter 3, item 233). Updated in the third addendum of this page.

partial quadrants and tuples

as in the book

to confirmA partial quadrant is a set $C = T^{-1}([0,\infty)^n \oplus W)$ for an sc-isomorphism $T : E \to \mathbb R^n \oplus W$; a tuple $(U, C, E)$ has $U = O \cap C$ with $O$ open.

closed and convex derived, not assumed$C^1$ a partial quadrant in $E^1$: V1.36
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §1.1, Definition 1.11, p. 10

A partial quadrant in an sc-Banach space $E$ is a closed convex subset $C \subset E$ such that there is an sc-isomorphism $T : E \to \mathbb R^n \oplus W$ with $T(C) = [0,\infty)^n \oplus W$. One considers tuples $(U, C, E)$ with $U$ a relatively open subset of the partial quadrant $C$.

Verified edition V1.10

In the sc-Banach space $\mathbb R^n \oplus W$ (with $\mathbb R^n$ constant) the quadrant on level $m$ is $\{(a, w) : a_i \ge 0 \text{ for all } i\}$; it is closed and convex with non-empty interior, and the level sets of the level-$0$ quadrant are the level quadrants. $C \subseteq E_0$ is a partial quadrant if there are $n$, an sc-Banach space $W$ and an sc-isomorphism $T : E \to \mathbb R^n \oplus W$ with $C = T_0^{-1}(\text{quadrant})$. Then every $C_m$ is closed, convex, with non-empty interior in $E_m$, and $C_m$ has unique differentiability (in Mathlib's sense) at each of its points; $E_0$ itself is a partial quadrant ($n = 0$). $(U, C, E)$ is a tuple, i.e. $U$ is a relatively open subset of the partial quadrant $C$, if $C$ is a partial quadrant and $U = O \cap C$ with $O \subseteq E_0$ open. Book: Definition 1.11, p. 10, and the sentence after it. Hidden hypotheses: none; "closed convex" is derived from the model. Deviation: none in the definition. The text's tacit use of $C_k$ as a partial quadrant in $E^k$ is V1.36 (for $k = 1$, and by iteration).

total maps $E_0 \to F_0$target enters only as $f(U) \subseteq U'$the text's $V$ is $U'$
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §1.1, Definition 1.12, p. 10

For tuples $(U, C, E)$ and $(U', C', E')$, a map $f : U \to U'$ is $\mathrm{sc}^0$ (sc-continuous) if $f(U_m) \subset U'_m$ and the induced maps $f : U_m \to U'_m$ are continuous for all $m \ge 0$.

Verified edition V1.11

For $f : E_0 \to F_0$ the level map $f_m : E_m \to F_m$ sends $x$ to the unique $y \in F_m$ with $\iota_m y = f(\iota_m x)$, when such $y$ exists (and to a junk value otherwise). $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^0$ on $U \subseteq E_0$ if for every $m$ and $x \in U_m$ the point $f(\iota_m x)$ lies in $\iota_m(F_m)$, and $f_m$ is continuous on $U_m$. Then $f$ is continuous on $U$; if $f(U) \subseteq V$ then $f_m(U_m) \subseteq V_m$; the property depends only on the values of $f$ on $U$ and passes to subsets of $U$; the composition of an $\mathrm{sc}^0$ map on $U$ with values in $V$ and an $\mathrm{sc}^0$ map on $V$ is $\mathrm{sc}^0$ on $U$; the identity and every sc-operator are $\mathrm{sc}^0$, the latter with level maps $T_m$. Book: Definition 1.12, p. 10: $f(U_m) \subset V_m$ (meaning $U'_m$) and $f : U_m \to U'_m$ continuous for all $m$. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): maps are total functions on $E_0$, and the target tuple enters only through $f(U) \subseteq U'$.

the tangent

as in the book

to confirmThe tangent $TE$ is $E^1 \oplus E$ and $TU = U^1 \oplus E$, with levels $U_{m+1} \times E_m$.

the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §1.1, Definition 1.13, p. 10

The tangent of $(U, C, E)$ is the tuple $T(U, C, E) = (TU, TC, TE)$ with $TU = U^1 \oplus E$, $TC = C^1 \oplus E$, $TE = E^1 \oplus E$. It is again a tuple: $TU$ is relatively open in the partial quadrant $TC$ of the sc-Banach space $TE$.

Verified edition V1.12

The tangent of an sc-Banach space $E$ is $TE := E^1 \oplus E$, with levels $E_{m+1} \times E_m$. For $U \subseteq E_0$, $TU \subseteq (TE)_0 = E_1 \times E_0$ is $\{(x, h) : x \in U_1\}$, with level-$m$ part $U_{m+1} \times E_m$; $U \subseteq V$ implies $TU \subseteq TV$. If $U$ is an sc-domain (V1.27), $TU$ is an sc-domain in $TE$; and the level-$1$ part of $TU$ is $T(U_1)$ in $T(E^1) = (TE)^1$. Book: Definition 1.13, p. 10: $T(U, C, E) = (U^1 \oplus E, C^1 \oplus E, E^1 \oplus E)$, "again a tuple". Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation: none; that $TC$ is a partial quadrant in $TE$, so that $T(U, C, E)$ is again a tuple, is V1.36, while the proofs of §§1.2–1.3 propagate the sc-domain property (V1.27) instead.

sc¹ maps and the tangent map

hypotheses explicit

to confirmA map is sc¹ on $U$ if it is sc⁰, differentiable from $U_1$ into $F_0$ at every point of $U_1$ with a derivative $Df(x)$ bounded on $E_0$, and $(x, h) \mapsto (f(x), Df(x)h)$ is sc⁰ on $TU$; $Df(x)$ is unique on relatively open subsets of partial quadrants; $x \mapsto Df(x)$ need not be norm continuous (an example on a weighted $c_0$ scale).

the family $Df$ is explicituniqueness of $Df(x)$ provedfinite dim. and compact-open: V1.34–V1.35not norm continuous: a $c_0$ example
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §1.1, Definition 1.14, pp. 10–11

$f : U \to U'$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ if (1) $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^0$; (2) for every $x \in U_1$ there is a bounded linear $Df(x) : E_0 \to F_0$ with $|f(x+h) - f(x) - Df(x)h|_0 / |h|_1 \to 0$ as $|h|_1 \to 0$, $h \in E_1$, $x + h \in U_1$; (3) the tangent map $Tf : TU \to TU'$, $Tf(x, h) = (f(x), Df(x)h)$, is $\mathrm{sc}^0$. In general $x \mapsto Df(x)$ is not continuous into $\mathcal L(E_0, F_0)$ with the operator norm, but it is with the compact-open topology; the $\mathrm{sc}^1$ maps between finite-dimensional spaces are the $C^1$ maps.

The text writes $Df(x)$ as if it were unique.

Verified edition V1.13

Let $f : E_0 \to F_0$, $U \subseteq E_0$ and $D : E_1 \to \mathcal L(E_0, F_0)$ a family of bounded operators. The tangent map $T_Df : (TE)_0 \to (TF)_0$ is $(x, h) \mapsto (f_1(x), D(x)h)$. $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$ with derivatives $D$ if (1) $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^0$ on $U$; (2) for every $x \in U_1$, the map $f \circ \iota_1 : E_1 \to F_0$ has derivative $D(x) \circ \iota_1$ at $x$ within $U_1$; (3) $T_Df$ is $\mathrm{sc}^0$ on $TU$. $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$ if some $D$ makes it so; Polyfold.scDeriv is a chosen such $D$ (junk if none exists) and Polyfold.tangentMap the tangent map built from it. If $D$ and $D'$ both satisfy (2) at a point $x \in U_1$ where $U_1$ has unique differentiability, then $D(x) = D'(x)$, because $E_1$ has dense image in $E_0$; hence on an sc-domain the chosen derivative agrees on $U_1$ with any admissible one, and the tangent map on $TU$. The property depends only on the values of $f$ on $U$. Level $0$ of condition (3) is the continuity of $(x, h) \mapsto D(x)h$ on $U_1 \times E_0$, and it implies: for $x \in U_1$, a compact $K \subseteq E_0$ and $c > 0$ there is $\delta > 0$ with $\|D(x')w - D(x)w\| \le c$ for all $x' \in U_1$ with $\|x' - x\|_1 < \delta$ and all $w \in K$ (continuity of $x \mapsto D(x)$ in the compact-open topology). It need not be norm continuous: on $E = \mathbb R \oplus X$, with $X$ the sc-Banach space whose level $m$ consists of the real sequences with $(k+1)^m x_k \to 0$, normed by $\sup_k (k+1)^m|x_k|$ (every level a copy of $c_0$, the inclusions $\mathrm{diag}(1/(k+1))$), the map $f(t, x)_k = \cos(kt)x_k$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ with $Df(t, x)(\tau, \xi)_k = -k\sin(kt)x_k\tau + \cos(kt)\xi_k$, and for every derivative family $D$ of $f$ the map $x \mapsto D(x)$ is not continuous on $E_1$ into $\mathcal L(E_0, X_0)$ with the operator norm: $(\pi/(n+1), 0) \to 0$ in $E_1$, but $\|Df(\pi/(n+1), 0) - Df(0, 0)\| \ge 2$. Book: Definition 1.14, pp. 10–11, with conditions (1)–(3) as stated, and the remarks that $x \mapsto Df(x)$ is continuous for the compact-open but not in general for the norm topology, and that sc¹ maps between finite-dimensional spaces are the $C^1$ maps. Hidden hypotheses: the uniqueness of $Df(x)$, without which "the tangent map" is undefined; it holds because $E_1$ is dense in $E_0$ and $U_1$ has unique differentiability (true for relatively open subsets of partial quadrants, V1.10). Deviation (hypotheses explicit): the derivative family is an explicit parameter of Polyfold.IsSc1With, with Polyfold.IsSc1 the text's notion. The compact-open remark is V1.34, its negative half the example above, which the text does not give (Findings, Chapter 1, follow-up item 1), and the finite-dimensional remark is V1.35 (on relatively open subsets of quadrants, with boundary; the open case is also in Polyfold/Test.lean, isSc1_iff_contDiffOn_of_finiteDimensional).

What differs (the comparison)

  • Condition (2) is Mathlib's differentiability of $f : U_1 \to F_0$ at $x$ within $U_1$, with derivative $Df(x)|_{E_1}$; the limit over $h \in E_1$ with $x + h \in U_1$ is exactly this.

That $x \mapsto Df(x)$ need not be norm continuous is proved by an example, which the text does not give: $f(t, x)_k = \cos(kt)x_k$ on $\mathbb R \oplus X$, $X$ the weighted $c_0$ scale (the project's first infinite-dimensional sc-Banach space); the factor $k$ of the $t$-derivative is absorbed by one level, $(\pi/(n+1), 0) \to 0$ in $E_1$, but $\|Df(\pi/(n+1), 0) - Df(0, 0)\| \ge 2$, and the derivative is unique on $E_1$, so no derivative family is norm continuous (Findings, Chapter 1, follow-up item 1; formerly G.3). sc^k and sc-smooth maps

as in the book

to confirm$f$ is sc^{k+1} if it is sc¹ with sc^k tangent map, and sc-smooth if sc^k for all $k$.

$Tf$ built from the chosen derivative
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §1.1, Definition 1.15, p. 11 (unnumbered in the preprint)

Inductively, an $\mathrm{sc}^0$ map $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^2$ if it is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ and $Tf : TU \to TV$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$; then $T^2f = T(Tf)$ is $\mathrm{sc}^0$, and $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^3$ if $T^2f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$, and so on. $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^\infty$, or sc-smooth, if it is $\mathrm{sc}^k$ for all $k \ge 0$.

The preprint's numbered Remark 1.15 (partial cones) is not formalized; the inductive definition that precedes it is numbered 1.15 here, as the Lean files do.

Verified edition V1.14

By recursion: $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^0$ on $U$ in the sense of V1.11; $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^{k+1}$ on $U$ if it is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$ and its tangent map (built from the chosen derivative) is $\mathrm{sc}^k$ on $TU \subseteq (TE)_0$ as a map into $(TF)_0$. $f$ is sc-smooth on $U$ if it is $\mathrm{sc}^k$ for every $k$. Then $\mathrm{sc}^{k+1}$ implies $\mathrm{sc}^k$, and $\mathrm{sc}^l$ for $l \le k$; $f$ is sc-smooth iff it is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ with sc-smooth tangent map; on an sc-domain, $\mathrm{sc}^k$ depends only on the values on $U$. Book: p. 11, the inductive definition after Definition 1.14 (numbered 1.15 here, as in the Lean files; the preprint's Remark 1.15 on partial cones is not formalized). Hidden hypotheses: none beyond V1.13.

Proposition 1.16

restated

to confirmAn sc⁰ map on an sc-domain is sc¹ iff on every level $f : U_{m+1} \to F_m$ is differentiable with a derivative extending to a bounded $Df(x) : E_m \to F_m$ that depends jointly continuously on $(x, h) \in U_{m+1} \times E_m$; then $f : U_{m+1} \to F_m$ is $C^1$, and $Df(x)$ is an sc-operator at smooth points.

the extensions $Df(x)$ an explicit familytheir compatibility across levels provedon any sc-domain
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §1.2, Proposition 1.16, p. 12

Let $U$ be relatively open in a partial quadrant of $E$ and $F$ an sc-Banach space. An $\mathrm{sc}^0$ map $f : U \to F$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ if and only if (1) for every $m \ge 1$, $f : U_m \to F_{m-1}$ is $C^1$, so that $df : U_m \to \mathcal L(E_m, F_{m-1})$ is continuous; and (2) for every $m \ge 1$ and $x \in U_m$, $df(x)$ extends to a bounded $Df(x) : E_{m-1} \to F_{m-1}$ with $(x, h) \mapsto Df(x)h$ continuous on $U_m \oplus E_{m-1}$. In particular, at a smooth point $x \in U_\infty$ of an $\mathrm{sc}^1$ map, $Df(x) : E \to F$ is an sc-operator.

Verified edition V1.15

Let $U$ be an sc-domain in $E$ and $f$ $\mathrm{sc}^0$ on $U$. Then $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$ if and only if there is a family $D_m(x) \in \mathcal L(E_m, F_m)$, $m \in \mathbb N$, $x \in U_{m+1}$, such that for every $m$: (a) $f_m \circ \iota : U_{m+1} \to F_m$ has derivative $D_m(x) \circ \iota$ at every $x \in U_{m+1}$ within $U_{m+1}$; (b) $(x, h) \mapsto D_m(x)h$ is continuous on $U_{m+1} \times E_m$. For any such family, $x \mapsto D_m(x) \circ \iota$ is continuous $U_{m+1} \to \mathcal L(E_{m+1}, F_m)$ in the operator norm, so $f : U_{m+1} \to F_m$ is $C^1$ within $U_{m+1}$; and $\iota_m D_m(x) = D_0(\iota x) \iota_m$, so all $D_m(x)$ are restrictions of the single operator $Df(x) := D_0(x)$. In the direction "sc¹ ⇒ levels" the family is the level operators of V1.26; in particular $f \circ \iota_1 : U_1 \to F_0$ is $C^1$. If $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ with derivatives $Df$ and $x \in U_1$ is a smooth point, $Df(x) : E_0 \to F_0$ is an sc-operator. Book: p. 12: an $\mathrm{sc}^0$ map on a relatively open subset of a partial quadrant is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ iff (1) for $m \ge 1$, $f : U_m \to F_{m-1}$ is $C^1$ with $df : U_m \to \mathcal L(E_m, F_{m-1})$ continuous and (2) $df(x)$ extends to a bounded $Df(x) : E_{m-1} \to F_{m-1}$ with $(x, h) \mapsto Df(x)h$ continuous on $U_m \oplus E_{m-1}$; in particular $Df(x)$ is an sc-operator at smooth points. Hidden hypotheses: the compatibility of the extensions $Df(x)$ across levels, which the text's notation assumes and the direction (⇐) needs (Lemma 3.H of the exposition); it is proved. Deviation (restated): the extensions form an explicit family; the $C^1$ property and the norm continuity of $df$ are consequences of (a)–(b) rather than part of the condition; the hypothesis on $U$ is the weaker sc-domain condition.

Let $U$ and $V$ be relatively open subsets of partial quadrants in sc-Banach spaces and $f : U \to V$ an $\mathrm{sc}^k$ map. Then $f : U^1 \to V^1$ is also $\mathrm{sc}^k$.

Then the level-$1$ map $f_1 : E_1 \to F_1$ is $\mathrm{sc}^k$ on $U_1$ as a map between the shifted sc-Banach spaces $E^1$ and $F^1$ (whose level sets of $U_1$ are the $U_{m+1}$). HWZ §1.2, Proposition 1.18, p. 13

Let $U$ and $V$ be relatively open subsets of partial quadrants in sc-Banach spaces. If $f : U \to V$ is $\mathrm{sc}^k$, then for every $m \ge 0$ the map $f : U_{m+k} \to V_m$ is of class $C^k$; moreover $f : U_{m+l} \to V_m$ is $C^l$ for every $0 \le l \le k$.

Let $U$ be an sc-domain in $E$ and $f$ $\mathrm{sc}^k$ on $U$. Let $U$ be relatively open in a partial quadrant of $E$ and $F$ an sc-Banach space. Assume that for every $m \ge 0$ and $0 \le l \le k$ the map $f : U \to F$ induces a map $f : U_{m+l} \to F_m$ of class $C^{l+1}$. Then $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^{k+1}$.

Verified edition V1.18

Let $U$ be an sc-domain in $E$ and $f$ $\mathrm{sc}^0$ on $U$. If for every $m \ge 0$ and $0 \le l \le k$ the map $f_m \circ \iota : U_{m+l} \to F_m$ (the level-$m$ map restricted along the inclusion $E_{m+l} \to E_m$) is $C^{l+1}$ within $U_{m+l}$, then $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^{k+1}$ on $U$; if this holds for every $l$, then $f$ is sc-smooth. Also proved, under the stronger hypothesis that every level map $f_m : U_m \to F_m$ is $C^{k+1}$ within $U_m$: $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^{k+1}$; for $k = 0$, where the two hypotheses agree, $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ with $Df(x)$ the derivative of $f : U_0 \to F_0$ within $U$ at $\iota_1 x$; and if $f$ maps $U_m$ into $F_m$ for every $m$ and every $f_m$ is $C^\infty$, then $f$ is sc-smooth. Book: p. 13: if $f : U_{m+l} \to F_m$ is $C^{l+1}$ for all $m \ge 0$ and $0 \le l \le k$, then $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^{k+1}$. Hidden hypotheses: none ("$f$ induces a map $U_{m+l} \to F_m$" is the $\mathrm{sc}^0$ hypothesis). Deviation: none; the sc-smooth statement is a direct consequence. Proof: the 2010 paper's (Proposition 2.4): $f$ is the elementary map with no vectors, and every elementary map with $j$ vectors and $j + s \le k + 1$ is $\mathrm{sc}^s$ (V1.38), with the derivatives $d^jf(x)$ supplied by the derivative tower of $f$ (V1.37). The induction cannot be run on the hypothesis itself: if $f$ satisfies it with $k$, then $Tf$ in general does not satisfy it with $k - 1$, since its second component $(x, h) \mapsto Df(x)h : U_{m+l+1} \times E_{m+l} \to F_m$ is only $C^l$. Under the stronger hypothesis the level maps of $Tf$ are $C^k$ and the induction is immediate.

Let $U$ be an sc-domain in $E$, $V$ a finite-dimensional normed space with its constant sc-structure and $f : E_0 \to V$. HWZ §1.3, Theorem 1.21, p. 13 (proof §1.4.2, pp. 15–16)

Let $U \subset C \subset E$, $V \subset D \subset F$ and $W \subset Q \subset G$ be relatively open subsets of partial quadrants in sc-Banach spaces and $f : U \to V$, $g : V \to W$ be $\mathrm{sc}^1$. Then $g \circ f : U \to W$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ and $T(g \circ f) = Tg \circ Tf$.

Remark 1.22: differentiability is guaranteed only with the loss of one level, yet the composition loses only one; the compactness of $E_{m+1} \to E_m$ saves the day.

Verified edition V1.20

Let $U \subseteq C \subseteq E$ and $V \subseteq D \subseteq F$ be relatively open subsets of partial quadrants, $G$ an sc-Banach space, $f : E_0 \to F_0$ $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$ with $f(U) \subseteq V$, and $g : F_0 \to G_0$ $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $V$. Then $g \circ f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$, and $T(g \circ f) = Tg \circ Tf$ on $TU$. More precisely: if $g$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $V$ with derivatives $Dg$, $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$ with derivatives $Df$, $f(U) \subseteq V$, and $V_1$ is the intersection of an open and a convex set, then $g \circ f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^1$ on $U$ with derivatives $x \mapsto Dg(f_1(x)) \circ Df(x)$, with no hypothesis on $U$; and $g \circ f \circ \iota_1$ has this derivative at every $x \in U_1$ within $U_1$. Iterated: if $U$, $V$ are sc-domains (in particular relatively open subsets of partial quadrants), $f$ $\mathrm{sc}^k$ on $U$ with $f(U) \subseteq V$ and $g$ $\mathrm{sc}^k$ on $V$, then $g \circ f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^k$ on $U$; sc-smooth maps compose to sc-smooth maps. Book: p. 13, with a third tuple $W \subset Q \subset G$ for the target of $g$; the proof is §1.4.2, pp. 15–16. Hidden hypotheses: the segment from $f(x)$ to $f(x+h)$ lies in $V_1$ for $|h|_1$ small, which uses the convexity of $D_1$, the openness of $V_1$ in $D_1$ and the continuity of $f : U_1 \to F_1$; the uniqueness of $D(g \circ f)(x)$ behind "$T(g \circ f) = Tg \circ Tf$". Deviation: none in the statement; $W \subset Q \subset G$ plays no role. Proof: the text's two integrals are replaced by the mean value inequality for $t \mapsto g(y_t) - t\,Dg(f(x)) (f(x+h) - f(x))$ on $[0, 1]$; the first integral is not needed since $Dg(f(x))$ is bounded on $F_0$; the uniform convergence on the compact closure of $\{Df(x)h/|h|_1\}$ is Mathlib's IsCompact.eventually_forall_of_forall_eventually rather than a subsequence argument. The text's appeal to Proposition 1.18 is not used.

HWZ §1.3, Definition 1.23, p. 14

Let $C$ be a partial quadrant in $E$ and $T : E \to \mathbb R^k \oplus W$ an sc-isomorphism with $T(C) = [0,\infty)^k \oplus W$. For $x \in C$ with $T(x) = (a_1, \dots, a_k, w)$ put $d_C(x) = \#\{i : a_i = 0\}$. The map $d_C : C \to \mathbb N_0$ is the degeneracy index; points with $d_C = 0$ are interior, with $d_C = 1$ boundary points, with $d_C \ge 2$ corners.

Verified edition V1.21

For $p = (a, w) \in \mathbb R^n \oplus W$ let $\#(p)$ be the number of $i$ with $a_i = 0$; for an sc-isomorphism $T : E \to \mathbb R^n \oplus W$ presenting a partial quadrant $C$ let $d_T(x) := \#(T_0 x)$. The degeneracy index $d_C : E_0 \to \mathbb N$ is $d_T$ for a chosen presentation $T$ of $C$ (and $0$ if $C$ is not a partial quadrant); for every presentation $T$ and every $x \in C$, $d_C(x) = d_T(x)$. On the quadrant itself $d(p) = \#(p)$. Book: p. 14: $d_C(x) = \#\{i : a_i = 0\}$ where $T(x) = (a_1, \dots, a_k, w)$; interior points, boundary points and corners. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation: none; $d_C$ is total on $E_0$ with junk values off $C$, and the classification into interior, boundary and corner points is terminology.

Verified edition V1.24

Let $E$, $F$ be real Banach spaces. A continuous linear $u : E \to F$ with closed range is a strict map; if moreover $\ker u$ is finite-dimensional and $\operatorname{range} u$ has finite codimension, $u$ is a Fredholm operator in Mathlib's sense. A continuous linear map of finite rank is a compact operator. For a compact operator $c : E \to E$: $\ker(1 + c)$ is finite-dimensional, $\operatorname{range}(1 + c)$ is closed and of finite codimension, and $1 + c$ is Fredholm. Compact-open lemma. Let $X$, $Y$, $Y'$, $Z$ be real normed spaces, $\iota : Y' \to Y$ a compact operator and $A : X \to \mathcal L(Y, Z)$. the Fredholm index and its invariance

to confirmThe index $\dim\ker - \dim\operatorname{coker}$ is additive under composition, and the Fredholm index between Banach spaces is invariant under small and under compact perturbations.

HWZ §1.4.1, p. 14 (quoted as classical)

Not stated. The proof of Proposition 1.10 uses that $T + S : E_m \to F_m$ is Fredholm; that its index is that of $T$ is the classical invariance of the index under compact perturbations, which the text does not invoke.

Verified edition V1.28

For a linear map $u : E \to F$ over a field let $\operatorname{ind}(u) := \dim\ker u - \dim(F/\operatorname{range}u) \in \mathbb Z$, meaningful when both dimensions are finite ("finite index"). If $u$ and $v : F \to G$ have finite index, so has $v \circ u$, and $\operatorname{ind}(v \circ u) = \operatorname{ind}(u) + \operatorname{ind}(v)$. If $a$ is bijective and $r$ has finite rank, $a + r$ has finite index $0$ (in particular $1 + r$). If $v \circ u$ and $u \circ v$ have finite index, so has $u$. For real Banach spaces $E$, $F$: a Fredholm operator $u : E \to F$ has finite index, and $\operatorname{ind}(u)$ is its Fredholm index. If $v : F \to E$ is a quasi-inverse of $u$ ($vu - 1$ and $uv - 1$ have finite rank) and $\|v\|\,\|s\| < 1$, then $u + s$ has finite index and $\operatorname{ind}(u + s) = \operatorname{ind}(u)$. If $u$ is Fredholm and $k : E \to F$ is compact, then $\operatorname{ind}(u + k) = \operatorname{ind}(u)$. Book: not stated; the classical fact behind the exposition's (F2) (Kato IV.5.26), which the text's §1.4.1 would need to conclude that the index is preserved. Deviation (not in the book): infrastructure Mathlib v4.33.1 lacks (it has Fredholm operators but no index). Proof: additivity by rank–nullity along the exact sequence $0 \to \ker u \to \ker vu \to \operatorname{range} u \cap \ker v \to F/\operatorname{range}u \to G/\operatorname{range}vu \to G/\operatorname{range}v \to 0$; small perturbations through $v(u + s) = (1 + vs) + (vu - 1)$ and $(u+s)v = (1 + sv) + (uv - 1)$, where $1 + vs$, $1 + sv$ are invertible by the Neumann series; compact perturbations by the local constancy of $t \mapsto \operatorname{ind}(u + tk)$ on $\mathbb R$ (each $u + t_0k$ is Fredholm by V1.25), not by Kato's argument.

Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation: none; $C^k$ for $k \ge 2$ is the iterate. These are the exposition's Lemmas 3.A(2) and 3.B, proved in the Chapter 2 files (Polyfold/Chapter2/LevelPolyfold.lean, Polyfold/Chapter2/TangentBundle.lean).

A derivative tower of order $k + 1$ for $f : E_0 \to F_0$ on $U$ consists of maps $\Phi_i : E_0 \times E_0^i \to F_0$ with $\Phi_0(x) = f(x)$ and, for $x \in U_{m+l}$, continuous $i$-linear maps $\Psi_{i,m,l}(x) : E_{m+l}^i \to F_m$, for $i \le l + 1$ and $i \le k + 1$, such that (a) $\iota_m \Psi_{i,m,l}(x)(h_1, \dots, h_i) = \Phi_i(\iota_{m+l} x)(\iota_{m+l} h_1, \dots, \iota_{m+l} h_i)$; (b) $\Psi_{i,m,l}$ is continuous on $U_{m+l}$ into the space of continuous $i$-linear maps; (c) for $i \le l$ and $i \le k$, $\Psi_{i,m,l}$ is differentiable within $U_{m+l}$ at every point, with derivative $\xi \mapsto \Psi_{i+1,m,l}(x)(\xi, \cdot)$. If $U$ is an sc-domain, $f$ is $\mathrm{sc}^0$ on $U$ and $f_m \circ \iota : U_{m+l} \to F_m$ is $C^{l+1}$ within $U_{m+l}$ for all $m$ and $l \le k$, then the iterated derivatives within the level sets, $\Psi_{i,m,l} := d^i(f_m \circ \iota)$ on $U_{m+l}$ and $\Phi_i$ the $i$-th derivative of $f : U_{i-1} \to F_0$ at lifts to $E_{i-1}$, form a derivative tower of order $k + 1$. In a tower, two values $\Psi_{i,m,l}(x)(h)$, $\Psi_{i,m,l'}(x')(h')$ with the same images in $E_0$ are equal. HWZ §2.2, Definition 2.11, pp. 23–24

A chart around $x$ in a space $X$ is $(V, \varphi, (O, C, E))$ with $V$ an open neighbourhood of $x$, $(O, C, E)$ an sc-smooth retract and $\varphi : V \to O$ a homeomorphism. Two charts are sc-smoothly compatible if $\psi \circ \varphi^{-1} : \varphi(V \cap V') \to \psi(V \cap V')$ and its inverse are sc-smooth (Definition 2.7); $\varphi(V \cap V')$ is a retract by Proposition 2.10(1).

Verified edition V2.10

A chart on a space $X$ is a local model $(O, C, E)$ and a partial equivalence $\varphi$ between $X$ and $E_0$ with open source $V$ and target $O$, continuous on $V$, with inverse continuous on $O$. The overlap $\varphi(V \cap V')$ is a retract. Two charts are compatible if $\psi \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is sc-smooth from $(\varphi(V \cap V'), C, E)$ to $(\psi(V \cap V'), C', E')$ and $\varphi \circ \psi^{-1}$ back. A chart is compatible with itself, compatibility passes to restrictions, and two charts each compatible with every chart of a family covering $V \cap V'$ are compatible. Book: Definition 2.11, pp. 23–24. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): the chart is a partial equivalence; the last statement, the locality of compatibility, is not in the text and is what makes the maximal atlas (V2.12) work.

An M-polyfold structure on a Hausdorff paracompact space $X$ is an atlas. $f : X \to Y$ is sc-smooth if for charts $\varphi$ around $x$ and $\varphi'$ around $f(x)$ with $f(V) \subseteq V'$, $\varphi' \circ f \circ \varphi^{-1} : O \to O'$ is sc-smooth (Definition 2.7); \"the definition does not depend on the choice of charts\".

Verified edition V2.33

Moreover, for every sc-smooth retraction $r$ in $C = T^{-1}([0, \infty)^n \oplus W)$ and every smooth $x \in O$ (no tameness), $T_xO$ and $T^R_xO$ are sc-subspaces of $E$ and $C_xO$ is a partial quadrant in the sc-Banach space $T_xO$ (with the sc-structure induced from $E$), of dimension $r = \operatorname{rank} M = \dim(T_xO/T^R_xO) \le d_C(x)$, where $M$ is the matrix of $Dr(x)$ on $E/E_x \cong \mathbb R^{I(x)}$. The core is Flor's theorem in the needed case: for a linear $M$ on $\mathbb R^\iota$ with $M^2 = M$ mapping the orthant into itself, the cone $\operatorname{range} M \cap [0, \infty)^\iota$ is the set of nonnegative combinations of linearly independent columns of $M$. Book: Remark 2.28, p. 33: the inclusions, and “naively one might expect that $C_xO$ is a partial quadrant in $T_xO$. However, this is in general not the case”, without an example. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (stronger): the remark's negative claim does not hold in our formal reading (checked in Lean); the remark may mean the narrower point below. Proof: $Dr(x)$ maps $C_x$ and $E_x$ into themselves (the sign arguments of Lemma 2.29), so $C_xO = Dr(x)(C_x)$; modulo $T^R_xO$ it is the column cone of the nonnegative idempotent matrix $M$, simplicial by Flor's theorem (minimal column supports, generation by descent on the support, independence through a private index of each minimal support); the sc-isomorphism $T_xO \cong \mathbb R^r \oplus T^R_xO$ of the proof of Theorem 2.31 (V2.42) carries $C_xO$ onto $[0, \infty)^r \oplus T^R_xO$. HWZ §2.4, Definition 2.34, pp. 39–40

An sc-smooth retraction $r : U \to U$ is tame if (1) $d_C(r(x)) = d_C(x)$ on $U$ and (2) at every smooth $x \in O$ there is an sc-subspace $A \subset E_x$ with $E = T_xO \oplus A$. A tame retract is the image of a tame retraction.

Verified edition V2.40

A retraction $r$ is tame for $T$ if (1) $d_C(r(x)) = d_C(x)$ for $x \in U$ and (2) for every smooth $x \in O_1$ there is a subspace $A \le E_x$ such that $E = Dr(x)E_0 \oplus A$ is an sc-splitting. $r$ is tame if it is tame for every presentation of $C$; tameness for one presentation implies it. A tame retract is the retract of a tame retraction. Identities of relatively open subsets are tame, and the restriction of a tame retraction to $U \cap r^{-1}(V)$, $V$ open, is tame. Book: Definition 2.34, pp. 39–40. Hidden hypotheses: that the definition does not depend on the presentation, which the text uses tacitly. Deviation (restated): none in substance.

For $P : Y \to X$ (Y paracompact Hausdorff, fibres Banachable), a strong bundle chart $(\Phi, P^{-1}(V), K, U \triangleleft F)$: $K = R(U \triangleleft F)$, $V$ open with a homeomorphism $\varphi : V \to O$, $\Phi : P^{-1}(V) \to K$ a homeomorphism covering $\varphi$, bounded linear on fibres. Verified edition V2.57

For $P : Y \to X$ with linear structures on the fibres: a strong bundle chart is a chart $\varphi$ of the M-polyfold $X$, an sc-Banach space $F$, a strong bundle retraction $R$ on a relatively open $U \subseteq C$ with base retract $O$, and a homeomorphism $\Phi : P^{-1}(V) \to K = R(U \times F_0)$ with $\Phi(y)_1 = \varphi(P(y))$ and linear on each fibre (hence continuous on fibres). Two charts are compatible if $\Phi' \circ \Phi^{-1}$ and $\Phi \circ \Phi'^{-1}$ are sc-smooth between the overlaps on $[0]$ and, through the lift to $F_1$, on $[1]$, and carry fibre components in $F_1$ to fibre components in $F'_1$. Atlases and their equivalence as in V2.11; two atlases are equivalent iff every chart of one is compatible with every chart of the other, and the relation is an equivalence relation (it rests on the locality of compatibility: near a point of the overlap a transition factors through a chart of the middle atlas, on $[0]$ and on $[1]$). A strong bundle chart restricts to every open $s \subseteq V$ (retraction domain $U \cap r^{-1}(W)$ for $\varphi(s) = O \cap W$, $K_s = \{(u, h) \in K \mid u \in \varphi(s)\}$, $\Phi$ unchanged), and restrictions of compatible charts are compatible. A space is Banachable if it is linearly homeomorphic to a Banach space. Book: Definition 2.50, pp. 51–52. Hidden hypotheses: $\varphi$ a chart of $X$ (the text: a homeomorphism onto $O$); the $[1]$-transition condition. Deviation (hypotheses explicit): both stated. The transitivity of the equivalence, which “an equivalence class of strong bundle atlases” (Definition 2.51) presupposes, and the restriction of charts, which the text uses silently (Lemma 5.2), are proved (Findings, Chapter 2, items 40, 42); a restriction whose retraction domain lies inside a given open $W \ni 0$ of $E$ is not, since $U \cap W$ need not be invariant under $r$.

HWZ §2.5, Definition 2.51 and the remarks after it, p. 52

A strong bundle over $X$ is $P : Y \to X$ (continuous surjection, $Y$ paracompact Hausdorff) with an equivalence class of strong bundle atlases. The charts induce a double filtration $Y_{m,k}$ and M-polyfolds $Y[i]$, $Y[i]_m = Y_{m,m+i}$; $P[i] : Y[i] \to X$ are sc-smooth.

Verified edition V2.58

A strong bundle is a continuous surjection $P : Y \to X$, $Y$ Hausdorff paracompact, with Banachable fibres and a strong bundle atlas. The charts $\Phi$ form an sc-smooth atlas of $Y$ (the M-polyfold $Y[0]$), and $P : Y[0] \to X$ is sc-smooth. $Y_{m,k}$ ($k \le m + 1$) is the set of $y$ with $\Phi(y) \in E_m \times F_k$ in the charts of the atlas around $y$; one chart around $y$ suffices. The charts $\Phi[1] : y \mapsto (\Phi(y)_1, \Phi(y)_2$ lifted to $F_1)$, defined on $Y_{0,1}$ with the topology they generate and onto the retracts $K[1]$, are pairwise compatible, their transition maps being the $[1]$-transitions of Definition 2.50, and make $Y[1]$ an M-polyfold; $P[1] : Y[1] \to X$ is sc-smooth. The charts of the strong bundle (compatible with the atlas) are those of the maximal atlas, which is equivalent to the given one: a chart is one iff it belongs to some atlas of the class, any two are compatible, restrictions of charts are charts, and equivalent atlases have the same charts. Book: Definition 2.51 and the remarks after it, p. 52. Hidden hypotheses: the paracompactness of $Y[1]$ (proved, V2.64); for the chart-independence of $Y_{m,m+1}$ and of $Y_{0,1}$, the $F_1$-condition on the $[1]$-transition (V2.57). Deviation (restated): $Y[1]$ carries the topology generated by the charts $\Phi[1]$, as $X_m$ in §2.2; the charts are those induced by the given atlas. The notions defined through the charts compatible with the atlas depend only on the class; those defined with the charts of the given atlas itself ($Y_{m,k}$, $Y[1]$ and its atlas, sc⁺-sections) are not shown invariant (Findings, Chapter 2, item 43).

HWZ §2.6.2, Theorem 2.55, p. 56

A paracompact Hausdorff space in which every point has a metrizable open neighbourhood is metrizable (quoted from Smirnov).

Verified edition V2.62

A paracompact Hausdorff space in which every point has a metrizable open neighbourhood is metrizable. More generally, a space $Y$ with open metrizable subspaces $V_i$ and a locally finite family of continuous $\rho_i \ge 0$ with $\operatorname{supp}\rho_i \subseteq V_i$, not all vanishing at any point, is metrizable, with the metric $\sum_i |\rho_i(x) - \rho_i(y)| + \min(\rho_i(x), \rho_i(y)) \min(d_i(x, y), 1)$; and if $\pi : Y \to X$ is continuous into a paracompact Hausdorff $X$ whose points have open neighbourhoods $U$ with $\pi^{-1}(U)$ metrizable, $Y$ is metrizable. Metrizable spaces are paracompact. Book: Theorem 2.55, p. 56, quoted from Smirnov. Deviation (stronger): proved, in the pull-back form used for $X_m$ and $TX$.

An sc-germ of neighbourhoods $\mathcal O(C, 0)$ around $0$ in a partial quadrant $C \subseteq E$ is a decreasing sequence $U_0 \supset U_1 \supset \cdots$ with $U_m$ a relatively open neighbourhood of $0$ in $C_m = C \cap E_m$; its tangent $T\mathcal O(C, 0)$ is $U_1 \oplus E_0 \supset U_2 \oplus E_1 \supset \cdots$. A relatively open $U \ni 0$ with $U_m = U \cap E_m$ is an example; \"the size of the sets $U_m$ does not matter\".

Verified edition V3.1

An sc-germ of neighbourhoods around $0$ in $C \subseteq E_0$ is a family $U_m \subseteq E_m$, each of the form $O \cap C_m$ with $O$ open in $E_m$, containing $0$, with $\iota U_{m+1} \subseteq U_m$. Its tangent germ has levels $U_{m+1} \times E_m$. A relatively open $U \ni 0$ in $C$ gives the germ $U_m = U \cap E_m$. $C$ is quadrant-like if $0 \in C$ and every $C_m$ is convex with nonempty interior; partial quadrants are. Book: Definition 3.1, p. 62. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): a germ is a fixed sequence, not a class up to shrinking; the text's "the size of the sets $U_m$ does not matter" is not built in, and the theorems say on which germ they hold. $(U_{m+1})_m$ is a germ only when all levels coincide (finite-dimensional $E$).

HWZ §3.1, Definition 3.3, p. 63

An sc-smooth section germ $(f, x_0)$ of $P : Y \to X$ is a continuous section $f : V \to P^{-1}(V)$ near the smooth point $x_0$ such that in a strong bundle chart with $\varphi(x_0) = 0$ the principal part $\mathbf f$ of $\Phi \circ f \circ \varphi^{-1} : O \to K$ has $\mathbf f \circ r : \mathcal O(C, 0) \to F$ an sc-smooth germ.

Verified edition V3.5

$(f, x_0)$ is an sc-smooth section germ of the strong bundle $P : Y \to X$ if $x_0$ is smooth and in some strong bundle chart compatible with the atlas, centred at $x_0$, the principal part $\mathbf f$ of $f$ satisfies: $\mathbf f \circ r$ is an sc-smooth germ on some sc-germ of neighbourhoods $G$ of $0$ with $G_0 \subseteq U$. An sc-smooth section is an sc-smooth section germ at every smooth point that has a centred chart (with the germ $U \cap E_m$). Book: Definition 3.3, p. 63. Hidden hypotheses: "a strong bundle chart" means a chart compatible with the atlas (a chart of the atlas need not be centred); the notion does not depend on the atlas within its class (Polyfold.StrongBundle.isChart_congr, V2.58). Deviation (hypotheses explicit): the chart, as just said. Since a fourth addendum the germ is the text's: $\mathbf f \circ r$ is an sc-smooth germ on some sc-germ of neighbourhoods $G$ with $G_0 \subseteq U$, whose levels may shrink with $m$, as for Definitions 3.4, 3.6 and 3.11 since phase 2. Until then it was required on the whole $U$ of the chart, which is stricter (a function $C^k$ on $(-1/k, 1/k)$ for every $k$ is an sc-smooth germ in the constant scale $\mathbb R$ and sc-smooth on no neighbourhood of $0$, Polyfold.exists_isScSmoothGerm_not_isScSmooth), and the item was "narrower". No theorem assumes the definition (Findings, Chapter 3, items 220–221, 260).

HWZ §3.1, the paragraph after Definition 3.4 and Proposition 3.5, pp. 64–65

If $f$ has the filling $g$ and $f(0) = 0$, then in the splittings $E = Dr(0)E \oplus \ker Dr(0)$, $F = \rho(0)F \oplus \ker\rho(0)$, $Dg(0) = \begin{pmatrix} Tf(0) & * \\ 0 & C \end{pmatrix}$ with $C$ an isomorphism, and (1) $Tf(0) : Dr(0)E \to \rho(0)F$ is onto iff $Dg(0)$ is; (2) $Tf(0)$ is Fredholm iff $Dg(0)$ is, with equal index.

Verified edition V3.8

Let $g$ be sc-smooth on $U$ and fill the section $f$ of $K \to O$, with $g(0) = 0$. Then $D(\rho(r(\cdot))g)(0) = \rho(0)Dg(0)$, $(1 - \rho(0))Dg(0)Dr(0) = 0$, $D(f \circ r)(0) = Dg(0)Dr(0)$; and $Tf(0) := Dg(0)$ restricted to $Dr(0)E \to \rho(0)F$ is surjective iff $Dg(0)$ is, Fredholm iff $Dg(0)$ is, and has the same index ($\dim\ker - \dim\mathrm{coker}$). The linear algebra holds for any idempotents $p$, $q$ and $L$ with $(1 - q)Lp = 0$ and $(1 - q)L : \ker p \to \ker q$ a topological isomorphism. In sc form: if $Dg(0)$ is an sc-Fredholm sc-operator, then $Dr(0)E$, $\rho(0)F$, $\ker Dr(0)$ and $\ker\rho(0)$ are sc-subspaces, $Tf(0) : Dr(0)E \to \rho(0)F$ is sc-Fredholm with the index of $Dg(0)$ on every level, and $(1 - \rho(0))Dg(0) : \ker Dr(0) \to \ker\rho(0)$ is an sc-isomorphism (condition (3) on every level); for $Dg(0)$ an sc-operator, $Dg(0)$ is sc-Fredholm iff $Tf(0)$ is sc-Fredholm and condition (3) holds on every level. Book: the paragraph after Definition 3.4 and Proposition 3.5, pp. 64–65. Hidden hypotheses: $(u, h) \mapsto \rho(u)h$ differentiable at $(0, 0)$; $g(0) = 0$. Deviation (stronger): the index equality without any finiteness assumption, via isomorphisms of kernels and cokernels instead of the text's factorization. The text's target "$(1 - D\rho(0))F$" is $(1 - \rho(0))F$. The sc form needs condition (3) only on level $0$, as the text states it (the higher levels of $Tf(0)$ come from the regularity of $Dg(0)$); its converse needs condition (3) on every level and fails with level $0$ alone (an example with the shift on a weighted $\ell^2$, not formalized; Findings, Chapter 3, items 234, 237, 238). The same holds for a filling germ (V3.7), with $Dg(0)$ the value at $0$ of any derivative family of $g$ (Polyfold.IsFillingGerm.proposition_3_5, Polyfold.IsFillingGerm.proposition_3_5_sc, Polyfold.IsFillingGerm.proposition_3_5_sc_iff; Findings, Chapter 3, items 272, 289, 314).

For a finite-dimensional $P$, a set $\widetilde C \subseteq P$, a finite-dimensional $Q$ and a germ $G$ around $0$ in $\widetilde C \oplus W$: $f$ is a basic germ with contraction map $B$ if $f$ is an sc-smooth germ on $G$ with $f(0) = 0$, the $W$-component of $f(a, w)$ is $w - B(a, w)$ on $U_0$, and $B$ is an sc⁰-contraction germ (V3.25). Book: Definition 3.7, p. 66 (Remark 3.8: historical). Hidden hypotheses: the points of the contraction estimate lie in $U_m$. Deviation (restated): $\mathbb R^n$, $\mathbb R^N$ replaced by finite-dimensional spaces.

HWZ §3.1, Definition 3.11, p. 69

$(f, x_0)$ is an sc-Fredholm germ if it has a filled version $(g, 0)$ and a local sc$^+$-section $s$ with $s(0) = g(0)$ such that $g - s$ is conjugated to a basic germ: a strong bundle isomorphism $\Psi : U \triangleleft F \to U' \triangleleft F'$ covering an sc-diffeomorphism $\psi$ with $\Psi \circ (g - s) \circ \psi^{-1}$ a basic germ.

Verified edition V3.13

$(f, x_0)$ is an sc-Fredholm germ if $x_0$ is smooth and in a strong bundle chart of $P$ centred at $x_0$ the principal part has a filling $g$ (V3.9: an sc-smooth germ on a germ of neighbourhoods inside $U$), there is an sc⁺-germ $s$ (IsScPlusGerm: $s : E_0 \to F_1$ an sc-smooth germ into $F^1$ on a germ inside $U$) with $\iota s(0) = g(0)$, and $k = g - \iota s$ is conjugated to a basic germ: strong bundle maps $\Psi : U \triangleleft F \to U' \triangleleft F'$ and $\Psi'$ back, inverse to each other, with base map $\psi$, $\psi(0) = 0$, $U'$ relatively open in $\widetilde C \oplus W$ ($\widetilde C$ a partial quadrant of a finite-dimensional space), a basic germ $h$ on a germ inside $U'$, and $(\Psi(u, k(u)))_2 = h(\psi(u))$ for $u \in U$ near $0$. Book: Definition 3.11, p. 69. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): the identity is required for $u \in U$; tameness unused; $C' = T\psi(0)C$ not imposed (it is proved, V3.48). The witnesses of the conjugation are also available as data (Polyfold.ConjugationData, V3.46). Since the switch to the text's germ reading (phase 2) the filling and the sc⁺-section are germs whose levels may shrink with $m$; $\Psi$ on all of $U$ is no restriction (on a relatively open $U_0 \subseteq U$ it is the same after restricting the chart on level $0$). The project's earlier notion, with $g$, $s$ sc-smooth on the whole $U$ (IsScFredholmGermWholeChart), implies this one and is exactly this one with $g$, $s$ sc-smooth on $U$; whether the two agree for sections sc-smooth on $X$ is open, and no theorem depends on it (Findings, Chapter 3, items 220–221, 261–264, 330). The existential over charts is essential: a filling in a chart gives a topological isomorphism $\ker Dr(0) \cong \ker\rho(0)$, a condition on the chart (Polyfold.IsFillingGerm.nonempty_kerEquiv), so a filling in one chart gives none in another unless these normal spaces match; a compatible tame chart of the trivial bundle carries no filling of any section (Polyfold.TrivialBundle.not_isFillingGerm_evenBundleChart; Findings, Chapter 3, items 350–352).

HWZ §3.1, Definition 3.21, pp. 76–77

A finite-dimensional sc-subspace $N \subseteq E$ is in good position to the partial quadrant $C$ if $N \cap C$ has nonempty interior in $N$ and $N$ has an sc-complement $P$ (a good complement) with: for some $\varepsilon > 0$, $|p|_0 \le \varepsilon|n|_0$ implies ($n \in C \iff n + p \in C$). A merely topological complement is allowed for non-smooth $N$.

Verified edition V3.20

A subspace $P$ is a good complement of $N$ with respect to $C$ if $E_0 = N \oplus P$ (algebraically) and for some $\varepsilon > 0$, $n \in N$, $p \in P$, $|p|_0 \le \varepsilon|n|_0$ imply ($n \in C \iff n + p \in C$). $N$ is in good position to $C$ if $N \cap C$ has nonempty interior in $N$ and $N$ has a good complement. Definition 3.21 as written (IsScGoodComplement: $E = N \oplus P$ an sc-splitting with the constant $\varepsilon$; IsInGoodPositionSc) implies this; on a partial quadrant a smooth finite-dimensional $N$ in good position is in good position with an sc-complement, also inside any sc-subspace $T \supseteq N$, and for smooth $N$ the text's good complements are the project's closed ones. Book: Definition 3.21, pp. 76–77 (an sc-complement, or a topological one). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (stronger): only the algebraic splitting is required, as a hypothesis. As a conclusion the algebraic form is weaker (an algebraic good complement need not be closed, round-trip item V3.20), so the text's form is formalized as well and proved where the theorems conclude good position (V3.47, V3.94; Findings, Chapter 3, items 210, 211).

$M \subseteq X$ (tame) has the $n$-dimensional tangent germ property if $M \subseteq X_\infty$ and every $x \in M$ has a chart $\varphi : (U, x) \to (O, 0)$ onto a tame retract $(O, C, E)$, an $n$-dimensional smooth $N \subseteq E$ in good position to $C$ with good complement $Y$, $E = N \oplus Y$, a relatively open $V \ni 0$ in $N \cap C$ and a continuous $\delta : V \to Y$ with (i) $\varphi(M \cap U) = \{v + \delta(v)\}$, (ii) $\delta : \mathcal O(N \cap C, 0) \to (Y, 0)$ an sc$^\infty$-germ, $\delta(0) = 0$, $D\delta(0) = 0$.

Verified edition V3.22

$M \subseteq X$ has the $n$-dimensional tangent germ property if $M \subseteq X_\infty$ and every $x \in M$ has: a chart $\varphi : (U, x) \to (O, 0)$ of $X$ onto a tame retract $(O, C, E)$; an $n$-dimensional smooth $N \subseteq E$ in good position to $C$ with a good complement $Y$ that is closed; a relatively open $V \ni 0$ in $N \cap C$; and a continuous $\delta : V \to E$ with values in $Y$, such that $\varphi(M \cap U) = \{v + \delta(v) \mid v \in V\}$, $\delta(0) = 0$, $D\delta(0) = 0$, and for every $m$, $k$ there is a relatively open $V_{m,k} \ni 0$ in $N \cap C$ with $\delta(V_{m,k}) \subseteq E_m$ and $\delta : V_{m,k} \to E_m$ of class $C^k$. HWZ §3.3, Definition 3.28, p. 85

An sc$^0$-germ $f : \mathcal O(\widetilde C \oplus W, 0) \to (W, 0)$ is an sc$^0$-contraction germ if $f(a, w) = w - B(a, w)$ and for every $\varepsilon > 0$, $m \ge 0$, $|B(a, w) - B(a, w')|_m \le \varepsilon|w - w'|_m$ for $(a, w), (a, w')$ on level $m$ sufficiently close to $(0, 0)$.

Verified edition V3.25

For a germ $G$ around $0$ in $\widetilde C \oplus W$: $B$ is an sc⁰-contraction germ if $B$ is an sc⁰-germ, $B(0, 0) = 0$, and for every $\varepsilon > 0$ and $m$ there is $r > 0$ such that the points $(a, w)$ with $a \in \widetilde C$, $|a| < r$, $|w|_m < r$ lie in $U_m$ and $|B(a, w) - B(a, w')|_m \le \varepsilon|w - w'|_m$ for such $(a, w)$, $(a, w')$. Every such $B$ has a working form: open $N(0) \supseteq N(1) \supseteq \cdots \ni 0$ in $P$ and $0 \in K(m) \subseteq O(m) \subseteq W_m$ ($K$ closed, $O$ open, $\iota K(m+1) \subseteq K(m)$) with $\{a\} \times O(m) \subseteq U_m$, $B_m(a, \cdot)$ a $\tfrac12$-contraction on $O(m)$ mapping $K(m)$ into itself, for $a \in N(m) \cap \widetilde C$. Book: Definition 3.28, p. 85. Hidden hypotheses: the points lie in $U_m$. Deviation (restated): explicit regions, needed for Lemma 3.31.

For a basic germ $f$ and the principal part $s$ of an sc$^+$-section with $s(0) = 0$ there is a strong bundle isomorphism $\Phi : U \triangleleft (\mathbb R^N \oplus W) \to U' \triangleleft (\mathbb R^{N'} \oplus W')$ covering an sc-diffeomorphism $\varphi$ such that $(\Phi_*(f + s))^1$ (levels raised by one) is a basic germ; $n - N = n' - N'$.

Verified edition V3.34

Let $f$ be a basic germ on $G$ with contraction $B$, $s$ an sc-smooth germ into $W^1$ with $s(0) = 0$ (the $W$-component of an sc⁺-germ), and $W = C \oplus X = R \oplus Z$ an sc-Fredholm splitting of $1 + D_2s(0)$ (it exists, Proposition 1.10). With $P_1 : W \to X$, $P_2 : W \to R$ the projections and $L = (1 + D_2s(0))|_X$, the linear maps $\psi(a, w) = ((a, (1 - P_1)w), P_1w)$ and $\Psi(q, w) = ((q, (1 - P_2)w), L^{-1}P_2w)$ carry $f + \iota s$ to the germ $\Psi \circ (f + \iota s) \circ \psi^{-1}$ on the index-raised spaces $(P \oplus C) \oplus X^1 \to (Q \oplus Z) \oplus X^1$, with germ $\psi(U_{m+1})$, which is a basic germ with contraction map $L^{-1}P_2(B - S)$, $S = s - D_2s(0)$; its zeros correspond to those of $f + \iota s$; and $\dim C = \dim Z$. Book: Theorem 3.38, pp. 90–93. Hidden hypotheses: the operator-norm continuity of the level derivatives of $s$ (for "$S$ is an arbitrarily small contraction"). HWZ §3.6, Proposition 3.52, p. 110

If $f$ is an sc-Fredholm section of the tame strong bundle $P : Y \to X$ and $f(x) = 0$, then $Tf(x) : T_xX \to Y_x$ is an sc-Fredholm operator (of the index $n - N$ of the basic germ, as the proof of Theorem 3.54 uses).

Verified edition V3.46

Let $f$ be a section of a strong bundle with $(f, x_0)$ an sc-Fredholm germ and $f(x_0) = 0$. In the strong bundle chart of Definition 3.11 centred at $x_0$, with the filling germ $g$ (a derivative family $Dg$ on a germ inside $U$) and the local sc⁺-germ $s$ for which $g - s$ is conjugated to a basic germ, $Dg(0) : E_0 \to F_0$ and $Tf(x_0) := Dg(0)|_{Dr(0)E_0} : Dr(0)E_0 \to \rho(0)F_0$ are Fredholm operators, and for every conjugation of $g - s$ to a basic germ $h : O(\widetilde C \oplus W, 0) \to \mathbb R^N \oplus W$, $\widetilde C \subseteq \mathbb R^n$, both have index $n - N$ (ConjugationData: the witnesses of a conjugation, Definition 3.11, as data). In particular $n - N$ is the same for all conjugations of one germ: for $k$ sc-smooth with $k(0) = 0$ and any conjugation of $k$ to a basic germ, $Dk(0)$ is Fredholm of index $n - N$. They are sc-Fredholm operators: $Dg(0) : E \to F$ is an sc-operator, $T_0O = Dr(0)E$ and $K_0 = \rho(0)F$ are sc-subspaces, and $Tf(x_0) : T_0O \to K_0$ is sc-Fredholm, both of index $n - N$ on every level; for an sc-Fredholm section the same holds in every strong bundle chart around a zero $y$, at the point $z$ over $y$, for $\mathrm{Lin}(z) : T_zO \to K_z$. Book: Proposition 3.52, p. 110 ($Tf(x) : T_xX \to Y_x$ is sc-Fredholm); the index $n - N$ is used in the proof of Theorem 3.54. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): in charts ($T_xX$ carries no linear structure here, Chapter 2). The hypothesis is the text's since the switch to the germ reading (phase 2): the filling and the sc⁺-section are germs (V3.13), and $Dg(0)$ is the value at $0$ of any derivative family of the filling germ; the forms for germ data on the whole chart are the _wholeChart declarations of the same names (Findings, Chapter 3, items 220–221, 289, 310, 331). Formerly "narrower", for that hypothesis. The sc-Fredholm property, first proved on level $0$ only, follows the text's argument with two steps it leaves out: $D(g - s)(0) = \Gamma(0)^{-1}Dh(0)D\psi(0)$ is sc-Fredholm by the criterion of V1.8, and $T_0O$, $K_0$ are sc-subspaces (Definition 2.47 at the smooth point $0$, the closed graph theorem); in other charts the levels are transported by the chart change at smooth points (Findings, Chapter 3, items 235, 239). The first version (Polyfold.proposition_3_52, kept for its consumers) states the index as "$n - N$ for some natural numbers $n$, $N$", which carries no information; proposition_3_52_index identifies $n$ and $N$ with the dimensions of the conjugating basic germ (Findings, Chapter 3, item 120). In every other strong bundle chart around $x_0$ the linearization is Fredholm of the same index (V3.96).

HWZ §3.6, Definition 3.53, p. 111

An sc-Fredholm germ $(f, x)$ of a tame strong bundle with $f(x) = 0$ is in good position if (1) $f'(x) : T_xX \to Y_x$ is surjective and (2) if $d_X(x) \ge 1$, $\ker f'(x)$ is in good position to the partial cone $C_xX$ in $T_xX$.

Verified edition V3.47

In a chart centred at the zero, with the filling germ $g$ and $Dg(0)$ the value at $0$ of a derivative family of $g$ (the same for all): the germ is in good position if $Tf(0) = Dg(0)|_{T_0O} : T_0O \to K_0$ is onto and $\ker Dg(0)$ is in good position to $T_0O \cap C$ inside $T_0O$ (interior of $\ker Dg(0) \cap C$ in $\ker Dg(0)$ nonempty, a good complement inside $T_0O$). For a section, $(f, x_0)$ is in good position if it has the data of Definition 3.11 at $x_0$ with the germ in good position in that chart. With the text's sc-complement (IsGoodPositionAtSc; for a section IsGoodPositionGermSc, in a tame chart) the kernel has a good sc-complement inside $T_0O$ ($T_m = N_m \oplus P_m$ on every level); at a zero of an sc-Fredholm section with tame germ data the two forms agree. Book: Definition 3.53, p. 111. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): in a chart rather than in $T_xX$; no case distinction $d_X(x) \ge 1$, which is recovered as a theorem for tame germ data: at a zero with $d_X = 0$ good position in a tame chart is the surjectivity of the linearization (V3.100). At a zero the linearization and the two conditions do not depend on the chart (V3.78); Definition 3.53 at a zero from a chart not centred there is V3.79, and in any chart of the germ data V3.107. The form in a tame chart, which the theorems of §3.6 assume and conclude, is V3.103. The germ data are the text's since the switch to the germ reading (phase 2, V3.13); the whole-chart forms are IsGoodPositionGermWholeChart, IsGoodPositionGermScWholeChart (Findings, Chapter 3, items 220–221, 280, 320, 330); that "an sc-splitting of $T_0O$", written in $E$, is an sc-splitting of the sc-Banach space $T_0O$ is not formalized (item 214).

HWZ §3.6, Theorem 3.54, p. 111 (proof pp. 111–115)

Let $f$ be an sc-Fredholm section of a tame strong bundle with $f(x) = 0$ and $(f, x)$ in good position. There is an open $V \ni x$ such that $S = \{y \in V \mid f(y) = 0\}$ has: (1) at every $y \in S$, $(f, y)$ is in good position; (2) $S$ is a sub-M-polyfold whose induced structure is equivalent to a smooth manifold with boundary with corners. The proof shows (3): $\psi\varphi(S) = \{v + \sigma(v) \mid v \in V'\}$ for the $\sigma$ of Corollary 3.47 applied to $\Psi_*(g) = h + t$.

Verified edition V3.48

Let $f$ be a section of a strong bundle, with $f(x_0) = 0$ and $(f, x_0)$ in good position in a tame chart (V3.103). Then there are: a tame strong bundle chart $\varphi$ centred at $x_0$ (compatible with the atlas, with tame base retraction); an sc-smooth $\psi$ on its $U$ with $\psi(0) = 0$ into a relatively open $U'$ of $\widetilde C \oplus W$ ($\widetilde C$ a partial quadrant), with an sc-smooth inverse $\psi'$ on $U'$; the data of Theorem 3.38 and a basic germ $h'$ with $D(h' + \iota t)(0)$ surjective and kernel $K$ in good position, $K$ a smooth subspace; a closed good complement $Y$ of $K$; a relatively open $V' \ni 0$ in $K \cap (\widetilde C \oplus W)$; $\sigma$ with values in $Y$ and $W$-components on level $1$, $C^1$ on $V'$, $\sigma(0) = 0$, $D\sigma(0) = 0$, such that every $v + \sigma(v)$, $v \in V'$, is a zero of $h' + \iota t$ in its germ, and for every $k \ge 1$ a $C^k$-lift $\sigma_k : V_k \to E'_k$ of $\sigma$ on a relatively open $V_k \ni 0$, $V_k \subseteq V'$ (Theorem 3.47 (1)); and an open $V_x \ni x_0$ in the chart domain on which $\psi\varphi$ is injective, $f(y) = 0 \iff (h' + \iota t)(\psi\varphi(y)) = 0$, and $\psi\varphi(\{y \in V_x \mid f(y) = 0\}) = \{v + \sigma(v) \mid v \in V'\}$. On the way: in the chart, $Dg(0)$ is surjective with kernel in good position to $C$ in $E$, $x \in C \iff D\psi(0)x \in C'$, and $D(\Psi_*g)(0) = \Gamma(0)Dg(0)D\psi(0)^{-1}$ is surjective Fredholm with kernel in good position. Book: Theorem 3.54, p. 111, the step (3) of its proof, pp. 113–114. Hidden hypotheses: the tameness of the chart at $x_0$, used only as $(1 - Dr(0))E \subseteq E_0$; the neighbourhood $V$ made explicit; the kernel is smooth (the text: without comment). Deviation (narrower): only the graph description (3) of the proof; conclusions (1) and (2) of the theorem are V3.82 and V3.85, the choice of $Y$ with the projection property V3.77.

There is $\rho > 0$ such that for $v \in N \cap C$ with $|v| < \rho$: $v + \tau(v) \in C$, and $Y$ is a good complement of $N_v = \{n + D\tau(v)n \mid n \in N\}$ with respect to the partial quadrant $C_{v + \tau(v)}$ (so $E_0 = N_v \oplus Y$, both closed, with the good-complement constant independent of $v$). HWZ §3.1, Theorem 3.19, p. 74

Let $X$ be an M-polyfold with $d_X \equiv 0$, $f$ an sc-Fredholm section of a strong bundle and $f(x_0) = 0$. Then $f'(x_0) : T_{x_0}X \to Y_{x_0}$ is sc-Fredholm. If it is surjective, there is an open $U \ni x_0$ such that $S(f, U) = \{y \in U \mid f(y) = 0\}$ is a sub-M-polyfold whose induced structure is that of a smooth manifold of dimension the Fredholm index, $f'(y)$ is surjective at every $y \in S(f, U)$, and $\ker f'(y) = T_yS(f, U)$.

Verified edition V3.68

Let $X$ be an M-polyfold with $d_X \equiv 0$, $f$ an sc-Fredholm section (V3.16) of a strong bundle $P : Y \to X$ with tame germ data (V3.103), $f(x_0) = 0$, and let $(f, x_0)$ be in good position in a tame chart (V3.47, V3.103) with a filler that satisfies condition (3) of Definition 3.4 at the zeros of the filler near $0$ (V3.82). Then there are an open $U \ni x_0$ and $d \in \mathbb N$ such that every zero $y \in U$ is a smooth point with $(f, y)$ in good position in a tame chart (in particular $f'(y)$ is onto), and $S(f, U) = \{y \in U \mid f(y) = 0\}$ is a sub-M-polyfold of $X$ whose induced structure (Proposition 2.21) is equivalent to that of a $d$-dimensional manifold with boundary with corners and has degeneracy index $0$ at every point. The first clause: for an sc-Fredholm section and a zero $x_0$ in good position, in the chart of Definition 3.11 centred at $x_0$, $Dg(0)$ and $f'(x_0) = Tf(x_0) = Dg(0)|_{T_0O} : T_0O \to K_0$ are sc-Fredholm operators with the same index $n - N$ on every level, and $Tf(x_0)$ is onto on every level (Polyfold.theorem_3_19_linearization_sc; Proposition 3.52 in sc form, V3.46); with no chart singled out, in every strong bundle chart around $x_0$ the linearization $\mathrm{Lin}(z) : T_zO \to K_z$ is an sc-Fredholm operator with the same index on every level (Polyfold.StrongBundle.linAt_isScFredholm, V3.96). Book: Theorem 3.19, p. 74 ("$f'(x_0)$ surjective"; the local solution set is a manifold of dimension the Fredholm index, $f'(y)$ onto and $\ker f'(y) = T_yS(f, U)$). Hidden hypotheses: tameness of the bundle, read as Definitions 3.50, 3.51 and 3.53 read it: germ data and good position in charts with tame base retraction (V3.103; the reading "every chart compatible with the atlas has a tame base retraction", under which this item was first proved, cannot be met, V3.104). Proof: Theorem 3.23 (V3.69) and Lemma 2.26 ($d_S \le d_X = 0$).

Let $f$ be an sc-Fredholm section of a tame strong bundle, $f(x) = 0$, $f'(x)$ surjective with kernel in good position to $C_xX$.
