HWZ §3.2, proof of Proposition 3.26, p. 80; §3.6, proof of Theorem 3.54, p. 114

Used without statement: in the proof of Proposition 3.26, “$X' = \psi(X)$ is tame”; in the proof of Theorem 3.54, the chart $\psi \circ \varphi$ onto $\psi(O)$ is a chart of the tame M-polyfold $X$.

Verified edition V3.71

Let $\psi : U \to U'$ be an sc-diffeomorphism between relatively open subsets of partial quadrants ($\psi$ sc-smooth on $U$, $\psi'$ sc-smooth on $U'$, mapping $U$ and $U'$ into each other, inverse to each other) and $r : U \to U$ a tame sc-smooth retraction onto $O$ whose domain is $U$. Then $r' = \psi \circ r \circ \psi'$ is a tame retraction of $U'$ onto $\psi(O)$, so $(\psi(O), C', E')$ is a tame retract; on the way $d_{C'}(\psi(x)) = d_C(x)$ (Theorem 1.25), $Dr'(y) = D\psi(x)Dr(x)D\psi'(y)$ at the level-$1$ points $y = \psi(x)$ with $x \in O$, and an sc-operator with an sc-operator inverse carries sc-subspaces and sc-splittings. The restriction of a tame retraction to $U \cap r^{-1}(W)$, $W$ open, is tame; an open subset $O \cap W$ of a tame retract is a tame retract; the model $\varphi(s)$ of a chart restricted to an open $s$ of its domain is tame if the model of $\varphi$ is. Book: used without statement in the proof of Proposition 3.26 ("$X' = \psi(X)$ is tame", p. 80) and in the proof of Theorem 3.54 (the chart $\psi \circ \varphi$ of a tame M-polyfold, p. 114). Hidden hypotheses: condition (2) of Definition 2.34 is transported at smooth points, where $D\psi(x)$ is an sc-isomorphism, with $D\psi(x)E_x \subseteq E'_{\psi(x)}$ (the one-sided sign argument). Deviation (not in the book).

HWZ §3.2, proof of Theorem 3.27, p. 84

In the proof of Theorem 3.27: $\delta$ is an sc$^\infty$-germ near every $v_0 \in V$. With the data $(\psi, N', Y', V', \tau)$ at $x_0 = \varphi^{-1}(v_0 + \delta(v_0))$, the map $w \mapsto \pi\varphi\psi^{-1}(w + \tau(w))$ has an invertible linearization at $0$, so it is a local diffeomorphism and $\delta$ is regular near $v_0$.

Verified edition V3.73

Let $\chi_1$, $\chi_2$ be charts of an M-polyfold $X$ and $S \subseteq X$. Suppose that $\chi_1(S \cap V_{x_1}) = \{v + \sigma_1(v) \mid v \in V_1\}$ for an open $V_{x_1}$ in the domain of $\chi_1$, where $K_1$ is a finite-dimensional smooth subspace in good position to $C_1$ with a closed complement $Y_1$, $V_1$ is relatively open in $K_1 \cap C_1$, and $\sigma_1$ has values in $Y_1$ and is of class $C^1$ on all of $V_1$; that $\chi_2$ is centred at a point $y \in V_{x_1} \cap V_{x_2}$ and $\chi_2(S \cap V_{x_2})$ is the graph of $\sigma_2$ over a relatively open $V_2 \ni 0$ in $K_2 \cap C_2$ (the same conditions on $K_2$, $Y_2$), with $\sigma_2$ continuous, $\sigma_2(0) = 0$, $D\sigma_2(0) = 0$ and $C^k$-lifts $\sigma_{2,k} : V_{2,k} \to E_{2,k}$ on relatively open neighbourhoods of $0$ for every $k \ge 1$; and that $\chi_1(y) = v_0 + \sigma_1(v_0)$, $v_0 \in V_1$. Then $\dim K_1 = \dim K_2$, and for all $m$, $k$ there is a relatively open $B' \ni v_0$ in $K_1 \cap C_1$, $B' \subseteq V_1$, on which $\sigma_1$ takes values in $E_{1,m}$ and is of class $C^k$ into $E_{1,m}$. On the way: a map differentiable on a set whose image has nonempty interior does not lower the dimension (Sard's lemma in fixed dimension); and a $C^k$ map between relatively open subsets of convex sets with nonempty interior in finite-dimensional spaces, with a continuous left inverse on its relatively open image and an invertible derivative at a point, has a $C^k$ inverse near the image of that point. Book: the step "$\delta$ is an sc$^\infty$-germ near every point $v_0 \in V$" of the proof of Theorem 3.27, p. 84. Hidden hypotheses: $\sigma_1$ differentiable at $v_0$ (here $C^1$ on $V_1$; without it the step fails, V3.24); $Y_1$, $Y_2$ closed; the lifts at $0$ (Theorem 3.47 (1), V3.42). Deviation (narrower): for two graph descriptions of one set, with $\sigma_1$ of class $C^1$ on $V_1$. Proof: the linearization of $\beta = \pi_1 \circ \chi_1\chi_2^{-1} \circ (1 + \sigma_2)$ at $0$ is injective by the chain rule for the transition and its inverse on level $1$ and the tangency of the graph of $\sigma_2$ to the retract; it is onto by the dimension count, not by the symmetric chain rule (which would need $\sigma_1$ differentiable into level $1$ at $v_0$); the inverse is $C^k$ by V3.90, not by Theorem 3.72 (which would need $d_C(x) = d_C(\beta(x))$).

In the proof of Theorem 3.27 the set $\Sigma = \{v + y \in C \mid v \in V, y \in Y\}$ is asserted to be relatively open in $C$; the retraction $t(v + w) = v + \delta(v)$ is defined on it.

ProjectsInto C N Y means: $z \in C$, $k \in N$, $z - k \in Y$ imply $k \in C$; for $E_0 = N \oplus Y$ the projection onto $N$ along $Y$ maps $C$ into $N \cap C$. If the finite-dimensional subspace $N$ is in good position to the partial quadrant $C$ of the sc-Banach space $E$, there is a continuous projection $\pi : E_0 \to N$ with $\pi(C) \subseteq N \cap C$ whose kernel $Y$ is a good complement of $N$; $Y$ is closed and ProjectsInto C N Y holds. The property is carried by continuous linear isomorphisms $S$ with $x \in C \iff Sx \in C'$. Book: not stated; the proof of Theorem 3.27 (p. 83) asserts that $\Sigma = \{v + y \in C \mid v \in V, y \in Y\}$ is relatively open in $C$, which fails for an arbitrary good complement (V3.24) and holds when $\pi(O) \subseteq C$. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (not in the book): the construction keeps the coordinates of a set $S$ of indices; when no coordinate vanishes at a nonzero point of $N \cap C$ and $N \cap C \ne N$, one coordinate is kept (the natural choice $S = \Sigma$ fails there: for $C = [0, \infty)^2$, $N = \mathbb R(1, 1)$, the projection along the good complement $\mathbb R(1, 2)$ maps $(0, 1)$ to $-(1, 1)$).

HWZ §3.4, Corollary 3.39, p. 93

If the sc-germ $g$ is equivalent by a strong bundle isomorphism $\Phi$ to a basic germ and $s$ is an sc$^+$-germ, there is a strong bundle map $\Psi$ such that $((\Psi \circ \Phi)_*(g + s))^1$ is a basic germ.

Verified edition V3.76

Let $U$ be relatively open in a partial quadrant of $E$ with $0 \in U$, $g : U \to F$ sc-smooth and conjugated to a basic germ (V3.13), and $s : U \to F_1$ sc-smooth into $F^1$ with $s(0) = 0$. Then the level-$1$ map $(g + \iota s)^1 : U_1 \to F_1$ is conjugated to a basic germ on the shifted structures $E^1 \triangleleft F^1$. Explicitly, for a conjugation $\Phi$ of $g$ to the basic germ $h$, with $t = \Phi[1]_*s$ ($t(0) = 0$) and $h' = h + (t_{\mathbb R^N}, 0)$, there are the data of Theorem 3.38 (V3.34) for $t_W$ such that: $h'$ is a basic germ and $\Phi_*(g + s) = h + t$ near $0$; the composite $\Gamma = \Lambda \circ \Phi^1$ of the index raise of $\Phi$ and the linear coordinate change $\Lambda$ of Theorem 3.38 is a strong bundle isomorphism of the shifted structures onto a relatively open subset of $(\widetilde C \oplus C) \oplus X^1$, with base map vanishing at $0$ and $\Gamma_* = \Lambda_* \circ \Phi^1_*$; and $(\Gamma(u, (g + s)^1(u)))_2 = (\Lambda_*(h + t))^1(\gamma(u))$ for $u \in U_1$ near $0$, a basic germ. The text's form "$\Gamma = \Psi \circ \Phi$, then raise the index" is the same map (compIso_eq_strongShift). On the way: a pair of sc-isomorphisms, the index raise of a strong bundle isomorphism and a composition of strong bundle isomorphisms are strong bundle isomorphisms, and push-forwards compose. Book: Corollary 3.39, p. 93. Hidden hypotheses: the index raise of a strong bundle isomorphism is one (used silently). Deviation (restated): "sc-germ" read as sc-smooth on $U$, $s$ as an sc⁺-map on all of $U$ with $s(0) = 0$; the conclusion is a conjugation of $(g + s)^1$ on the shifted structures; the text's "strong bundle map $\Psi$" is an isomorphism; the $\mathbb R^N$-component of $t$ is absorbed into $h$; the text's $\tau : Z \to C$ is not applied.

the linearization at a zero in charts, and its chart independence

to confirmAt a zero, the linearizations in two strong bundle charts are conjugate by isomorphisms respecting the partial quadrants: surjectivity, Fredholm index and good position of the kernel do not depend on the chart.

HWZ §3.6, Definition 3.53, p. 111; §2.4, Definition 2.38, p. 42

Definition 3.53 is stated with $f'(x) : T_xX \to Y_x$ and the partial cone $C_xX$; Definition 2.38 asserts that $T^R_xX$ and $C_xX$ do not depend on the chart (Proposition 2.30). The linearization is defined at the centre of a chart, through a filler.

Verified edition V3.78

In a strong bundle chart (retraction $r$ on $U$ onto $O$, fibre projections $\rho$, principal part $\mathbf f$), $\mathrm{Lin}(z) = D(\mathbf f \circ r)(z)|_{T_zO}$, $T_zO = Dr(z)E$, at every level-$1$ point $z$ of the retract. At a zero its values lie in $K_z = \rho(z)F$; it equals $Dg(z)$ on $T_zO$ for every $g$ sc¹ on $U$ agreeing with $\mathbf f$ on $O$ near $z$, and for every sc¹-germ $g$ agreeing with $\mathbf f$ near $z$ with $z$ in its germ ($Dg(z)$ the value of its derivative family; Findings, Chapter 3, item 284); at a centred zero it is the $Tf(0)$ of Proposition 3.5 (V3.8), also for a filling germ. For strong bundle charts $c$, $c'$ whose transition is sc-smooth on $[0]$, a section with sc-smooth principal parts in both, and a zero $y$ in both domains with level-$1$ points $z$, $z'$ over $\varphi(y)$, $\varphi'(y)$: there are topological linear isomorphisms $A : T_zO \to T_{z'}O'$ and $\Gamma : K_z \to K'_{z'}$ with $\Gamma \circ \mathrm{Lin}(z) = \mathrm{Lin}'(z') \circ A$ and, on $T_zO$, $x \in C_z \iff Ax \in C'_{z'}$ (the partial quadrants at the two points). Hence for two strong bundle charts of $P$ and an sc-smooth section, $\mathrm{Lin}(z)$ and $\mathrm{Lin}'(z')$ are simultaneously onto, simultaneously Fredholm with the same index, and their kernels are simultaneously in good position to the partial quadrants inside $T_zO$, $T_{z'}O'$ (good position inside a subspace is carried by isomorphisms respecting the cones). Book: Definition 3.53 (p. 111) presupposes it; Definition 2.38 (p. 42) asserts the chart independence of $T^R_xX$, $C_xX$ by Proposition 2.30; nothing is said about $f'(x)$. Hidden hypotheses: the point is a zero (away from zeros the linearization is not chart independent). Deviation (not in the book): the chart form of what gap G.13 leaves open; of the compatibility of Definition 2.50 only the sc-smoothness of the transition on $[0]$ is used; level-$1$ points suffice; no tameness.

(a) Let $C \subseteq V$ be closed under nonnegative scaling with $0 \in C$ and $N \subseteq V$ a subspace. In the coordinates of the text's proof — $E = \mathbb R^n \oplus X$ ($\mathbb R^n$ any finite-dimensional space with a partial quadrant $\widetilde C$), $C = \widetilde C \oplus X$, $F = \mathbb R^N \oplus Y$ — let $U$ be relatively open in $C$ with $0 \in U$ and $f : U \to F$ sc-smooth; let $V_o \ni 0$ be open in $\mathbb R^n$ with $(b, 0) \in U$ for $b \in V_o \cap \widetilde C$, and $L(b) : X \to Y$ sc-isomorphisms with $L(b)h = (Df(b, 0)(0, h))_Y$ on level $0$ and lower bounds $c_m|h|_m \le |L(b)h|_m$ for $b \in V_o \cap \widetilde C$, $h \in X_m$, every $m$; and let condition (3) hold (DerivCondition: for all $m$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $r > 0$ with $|[D_2f(b, 0) - D_2f(b, x)]h|_m \le \varepsilon|h|_m$ for $b \in \widetilde C$, $|b| < r$, $x \in X_{m+1}$, $|x|_m < r$, $(b, 0), (b, x) \in U$, $h \in X_m$). Then on $U' = U \cap (V_o \oplus X)$: $k(b, x) = ((f(b, x) - f(0))_{\mathbb R^N}, L(b)^{-1}(f(b, x) - f(0))_Y)$ is a basic germ with contraction map $H(b, x) = x - L(b)^{-1}(f(b, x) - f(0))_Y$; $\Phi((b, x), (c, y)) = ((b, x), (c, L(b)^{-1}y))$ is a strong bundle isomorphism $U' \triangleleft (\mathbb R^N \oplus Y) \to U' \triangleleft (\mathbb R^N \oplus X)$ covering the identity; and $f - f(0)$ is conjugated to a basic germ. For $U$ relatively open and convex in a partial quadrant $C \subseteq \mathbb R^n$, $f : U \to C$ smooth with $\|Df - 1\| \le \tfrac12$, $f(0) = 0$ and $d_C(x) = d_C(f(x))$: $f(U)$ is relatively open and $f : U \to f(U)$ is a smooth diffeomorphism (Lemma 3.77: the inverse is differentiable with $Dg = [Df \circ g]^{-1}$).

Let $U$ be a convex subset of a finite-dimensional normed space $V$ with unique differentiability at its points, $f : V \to V$ of class $C^j$ ($j \ge 1$) on $U$ with $\|Df(x) - 1\| \le \tfrac12$ for $x \in U$, and let $f(U)$ have unique differentiability. Then $f$ is injective on $U$ ($\tfrac12|x - x'| \le |f(x) - f(x')|$), its inverse $g$ is differentiable within $f(U)$ with $Dg(y) = [Df(g(y))]^{-1}$, and $g$ is of class $C^j$ on $f(U)$. Let $\mathbb R^n$ carry its M-polyfold structure with the constant sc-structure and the charts $r \mapsto r - r_0$, $\mathbb R^n \times X$ the product M-polyfold, $\pi(r, x) = x$, and $\pi^P : \pi^*Y \to \mathbb R^n \times X$ the pull-back strong bundle with the natural structure of Proposition 2.54 (the atlas of all charts pulled back from charts of $P$ through charts of $\mathbb R^n \times X$). In sc form, at every zero in $V_x$ and in every chart, $\mathrm{Lin}(z)$ is sc-Fredholm, onto on every level, of index $d$ on every level (theorem_3_54_index_locally_constant_sc); at any zero of an sc-Fredholm section, in every chart, $\mathrm{Lin}(z)$ is sc-Fredholm with the same index on every level (linAt_isScFredholm). What differs (the comparison)

  • Proposition 6.2 is proved with the text’s hypotheses (fifth addendum of this page; in the fourth, with bump functions), by the text’s device run on the restriction $P|V$ of $P$ to the domain $V$ of a strong bundle chart around $\varphi(t_0)$ (StrongBundle.restrictOpen), for each $t_0$: an sc$^+$-section $S$ of the pull-back to $\mathbb R \times V$ with $\tilde f + S = 0$ along the graph of the path near $t_0$ (the text’s $s(t, x) = R(x, f(\varphi(t)))$ in the chart, with no cut-off, since the chart covers $V$), the local constancy of the index of $\tilde f + S$ along its zero set (stabilizing sections $R(\cdot, e_i)$ in the product chart, again without cut-off, and the implicit function theorem), the index count $\mathrm{ind}(\tilde f + S)'(t, x) = \mathrm{ind}(f, x) + 1$ through the slice $S(t, \cdot)$ (isIndexAt_of_pullback_isLinOfIndex), and the connectedness of $\mathbb R$ (proposition_6_2_local). No bump functions are assumed (“we do not need a sc-smooth partition of unity”, p. 202); tame germ data are the project’s reading of the text’s tameness (V3.103), as in V3.94, where they are no narrowing. With bump functions the proposition holds for the global reading of Definition 6.1 as well (proposition_6_2, the form of the fourth addendum, whose section along the path is cut off by a bump; exists_isScPlusSection_pullback_of_path) (Findings, Chapter 3, items 340–349, 360–367).
  • Why still “narrower”. The path is $\varphi : \mathbb R \to X$, not $[0, 1] \to X$: $\mathbb R \times X$ is the product of Theorem 3.18 and has no boundary, and the text’s tame M-polyfold $[0, 1] \times X$ is not used. A path on $[0, 1]$ that extends sc-smoothly to $\mathbb R$ is covered; a path sc-smooth on $[0, 1]$ only, in the sense of M-polyfolds with boundary, is not, and the project has no M-polyfold $[0, 1]$. This is the one narrowing left: the bump functions are gone, Definition 6.1 has the text’s local sections, and the hypotheses on $f$ are the text’s in the project’s reading of tameness.
  • Definition 6.1 has no row of its own. It is IsIndexAtLocal: the text’s locally defined sc$^+$-section is a section of the restriction $P|V$ to an open $V \ni x$ — the restriction of a strong bundle to an open set, which the text uses without comment, is constructed (StrongBundle.restrictOpen, whose atlas consists of the charts of $P$ inside $V$) — and the text’s $f - s$, $s(x) = f(x)$, is written $f + s$, $(f + s)(x) = 0$. It is well defined, two local sections being compared on the intersection of their domains (IsIndexAtLocal.unique), and it exists at every smooth point without bump functions, through the section $-R(\cdot, f(x))$ on a chart domain (exists_isIndexAtLocal). The global reading IsIndexAt of the fourth addendum implies it, and when $X$ admits bump functions the two agree, the local section being cut off (isIndexAtLocal_iff_isIndexAt). The independence of $s$ is proved from the germ data and Theorem 3.15, without the text’s appeal to Proposition 1.10, for which the project has no lemma that the linearization of an sc$^+$-section is compact (Findings, Chapter 3, items 340, 364, 367).
  • Along the solution set the formal proof combines the good position of the nearby zeros (V3.94), the local constancy of the dimension (V3.85) and dimension = index at each zero (V3.97); the text’s proof of Proposition 6.2 uses the step of V3.82 for an extended section, which along solution sets is repaired by V3.93 (Findings, Chapter 3, items 171, 188). Added in the second addendum of this page.
  • Updated after the repair of the tameness hypothesis: first proved with “the base retraction of every strong bundle chart compatible with the atlas is tame” (htame), which no strong bundle over a nonempty base satisfies (V3.104), so that form was vacuous; now with the hypotheses of V3.103 (Findings, Chapter 3, items 190–192).
  • The sc form (the index of $f'(y)$ as an sc-Fredholm operator, on every level, in every chart) is proved as well; that $\mathrm{Lin}(z)$ is sc-Fredholm at every zero in every chart, with the level-$0$ index on every level, is StrongBundle.linAt_isScFredholm (V3.96), cited here since the fifth addendum. The local constancy without good position holds with the text’s hypotheses (tame germ data, no bump functions; index_locally_constant_tame, in sc form theorem_3_54_index_locally_constant_general_tame), by the text’s device for Proposition 6.2 on the restriction $P|V$ to a chart domain: finitely many sc$^+$-sections $R(\cdot, e_i)$, which on $P|V$ need no cut-off, put the parametrized section of Theorem 3.18 into general position at $(0, x_0)$, its index is constant along its solution set (the case above), at $(0, y)$ it is $k + \operatorname{ind} f'(y)$, and the index at a zero is the same for $P$ and $P|V$, through the germ datum (Findings, Chapter 3, items 240–242, 360–363). The first proof, for M-polyfolds admitting bump functions (Lemma 5.11 for the sections), is kept (index_locally_constant_of_admitsBumpFunctions). The candidate counterexample of items 188 and 243 is excluded under tame germ data by Theorem 3.54 (1). Without tame germ data the question is open: $\operatorname{ind} f'(y) = \operatorname{ind} f'(x_0)$ iff the block $C(z) = (1 - \rho(z))Dg(z)|_{\ker Dr(z)}$ of the filling has index $0$, which condition (3) of Definition 3.4 gives at $z = 0$ only (items 243, 343). Updated in the third, fourth and fifth addenda of this page.

Let $f$ be an sc-Fredholm section of a strong bundle with tame germ data (V3.103) and $y$ a zero with $d_X(y) = 0$. Then $(f, y)$ is in good position in a tame chart if and only if IsLinSurjAt f y. HWZ §3.6, Definitions 3.50, 3.51, p. 110; Definition 3.53, p. 111

(3.50) For an sc-smooth section $f$ of the tame strong bundle $P : Y \to X$ and a smooth point $x$: $(f, x)$ is an sc-Fredholm germ if there is a strong bundle chart $\Phi : \Phi^{-1}(V) \to K$ around $x$ covering $\varphi : (V, x) \to (O, 0)$, “where $K \to O$ is a tame strong local bundle”, in which the local section has a filling $g$ near $0$ and a local sc$^+$-section $s$ with $s(0) = g(0)$ and $g - s$ conjugated near $0$ to a basic germ. (3.51) An sc-smooth section of the tame strong bundle is sc-Fredholm if it is regularizing and an sc-Fredholm germ at every smooth point. (3.53) Good position is defined for an sc-Fredholm germ of a tame strong bundle. A strong bundle retraction is tame when its base retraction $r$ is (p. 49).

A strong bundle chart of $P$ is tame (IsTameChart) if it is compatible with the atlas and its base retraction $r : U \to U$ is tame (Definition 2.34). IsScFredholmGermTame f x (Definition 3.50, "tame germ data at $x$"): $x$ is a smooth point and there are the data of Definition 3.11 (V3.13: a strong bundle chart centred at $x$, a filling germ $g$ of the principal part, a local sc⁺-germ $s$ with $s(0) = g(0)$, and $g - s$ conjugated near $0$ to a basic germ; the text's germ reading) in a tame chart. IsGoodPositionGermTame f x ("good position in a tame chart"): the same data with the germ in good position in that chart (Definition 3.53 in the chart form of V3.47). IsScFredholmSectionTame f (Definition 3.51, "tame germ data"): $f$ is an sc-Fredholm section (V3.16) with tame germ data at every smooth point. Each of these implies the form without tameness (V3.13, V3.47), good position in a tame chart gives tame germ data, and the strengthened good position of V3.82 is stated in a tame chart and implies good position in it. A retraction agreeing on its domain with a tame retraction is tame; hence a compatible chart whose base retraction is the identity of $U$ (the retract $O = U$ relatively open in the partial quadrant) is tame, so the hypotheses can be met. Book: Definition 3.50, p. 110 (a strong bundle chart around $x$ "where $K \to O$ is a tame strong local bundle", as in Definition 3.6, p. 66); Definition 3.51, p. 110, and Definition 3.53, p. 111 (for a tame strong bundle); a strong bundle retraction is tame when its $r$ is (p. 49); the proof of Proposition 3.52 starts from "a tame strong bundle chart" (p. 110). Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (hypotheses explicit): these are the hypotheses of the implicit function theorems of §3.6 (V3.48, V3.68–V3.70, V3.80–V3.82, V3.84–V3.87, V3.94–V3.102), in place of the reading of "tame strong bundle" as the tameness of the base retraction of every compatible chart, under which they were first proved and which cannot be met (V3.104). Whether germ data in some chart (V3.13) can be moved to some compatible tame chart when the atlas consists of tame charts is open; it cannot be done by re-centring a chart of the tame atlas, since whether a filling exists in a chart depends on the chart: the trivial bundle with a one-chart tame atlas has sc-Fredholm sections with tame germ data in compatible charts and no germ data in the chart of the atlas (Findings, Chapter 3, items 350–353). The text builds the tame chart into Definition 3.50, and so do the theorems. Since the switch to the text's germ reading (phase 2) the three notions carry the text's germ data (V3.13, V3.45); the earlier whole-chart forms are IsScFredholmGermTameWholeChart, IsGoodPositionGermTameWholeChart, IsScFredholmSectionTameWholeChart, and the non-vacuity witnesses satisfy both readings (Findings, Chapter 3, items 220–221, 304, 330). For Definition 3.53 the comparison is that of V3.47. Formerly "restated", for the whole-chart reading (round-trip item V3.103).

Verified edition V3.104

Let $W$ be an sc-Banach space and $c$ the constant retraction $(a, w) \mapsto (1, 0)$ of the partial quadrant $[0, \infty) \oplus W$ of $\mathbb R \oplus W$ (sc-smooth, $(1, 0)$ being a smooth point), with retract $\{(1, 0)\}$. For every sc-smooth retraction $r$ of a nonempty relatively open subset $U$ of a partial quadrant $C$, the product retraction $c \times r$ of $([0, \infty) \oplus W) \times U$, whose retract is $\{(1, 0)\} \times r(U)$, is not tame: at $((0, 0), u)$ with $u \in r(U)$ the degeneracy index is $1 + d_C(u)$, at its image $((1, 0), u)$ it is $d_C(u)$, against condition (1) of Definition 2.34. Book: not in the text (Definition 2.34, pp. 39–40; Definition 2.50, pp. 51–52). Hidden hypotheses: none. That chart and its compatibility are not formalized (see "What is not verified"); so the earlier statements, vacuous by this argument, are replaced by those with tame germ data (V3.103).

Definition 4.1, corner charts and corner structures

restated

to confirmA corner chart is a chart onto a relatively open subset of a partial quadrant in a finite-dimensional space with the constant structure; a corner structure is an equivalent atlas of corner charts, of possibly varying dimension, and makes $X$ tame.

compatibility = equivalence of atlasesdimension may vary
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §4.1, Definition 4.1, p. 147

An M-polyfold $X$ has a compatible smooth manifold structure with boundary with corners if it admits an atlas of sc-smoothly compatible charts $(V, \varphi, (U, C, \mathbb R^n))$, $\varphi : V \to U$ an sc-diffeomorphism from an open $V \subseteq X$ onto a relatively open subset $U$ of a partial quadrant $C$ in $\mathbb R^n$ (or in a finite-dimensional vector space).

Verified edition V4.1

A chart of $X$ is a corner chart if its local model is $(U, C, V)$ with $V$ a finite-dimensional real normed space carrying the constant sc-structure, $C$ a partial quadrant in $V$, $U$ relatively open in $C$, and the identity retraction. $X$ has a corner structure if it has an atlas of corner charts equivalent to its atlas; equivalently, every point of $X$ lies in a corner chart that is a chart of the M-polyfold structure. The dimension of $V$ may vary from chart to chart. The model of a corner chart is a tame retract and an sc⁺-retract, and an M-polyfold with a corner structure is tame. Book: Definition 4.1, p. 147. Hidden hypotheses: "sc-smoothly compatible charts" with "$\varphi$ an sc-diffeomorphism" is read as compatibility with the atlas of $X$ (equivalence of atlases, as for tameness). Deviation (restated): the classical manifold structure with corners is represented by the atlas of corner charts; local constancy of the dimension is neither stated by the text nor formalized.

For a tame M-polyfold $X$ the following are equivalent. (i) $X$ has a compatible smooth manifold structure with boundary with corners. Remark 4.3

stronger

to confirm$1_1^0 : X^1 \to X$ is sc-smooth; if $X = X_1$ and $1_0^1$ is sc-smooth it is an sc-diffeomorphism; some M-polyfold with $X_0 = X_\infty$ has $1_0^1$ not sc-smooth; a finite-dimensional space with the constant structure has $V^1 = V$, and all its retracts are sc⁺-retracts.

“$X^1 \ne X$”: an example (G.31)$X = X_1$ in place of $X_0 = X_\infty$even the topologies of $X$, $X^1$ differ
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §4.1, Remark 4.3, p. 148

If $X_0 = X_\infty$, $1_0^1 : X \to X^1$ has the inverse $1_1^0$, which is always sc-smooth; so if $1_0^1$ is sc-smooth it is an sc-diffeomorphism. It is possible that $X^1 \ne X$ as M-polyfolds although the underlying sets agree. A finite-dimensional space with the constant structure has $X = X^1$.

Verified edition V4.6

The inclusion $1_1^0 : X^1 \to X$ is always sc-smooth; in the charts $(V_1, \varphi, (O_1, C_1, E^1))$ and $\varphi$ it is the sc-operator $\iota : E^1 \to E$. If every point of $X$ lies in $X_1$ and $1_0^1 : X \to X^1$ is sc-smooth, then $1_0^1$ is an sc-diffeomorphism with inverse $1_1^0$. For a finite-dimensional $V$ with the constant structure, $V^1 = V$ as sc-Banach spaces, the lift $V \to V^1$ is the identity, and every sc-smooth retract in $V$ is an sc⁺-retract. The levels of $X^1$ are those of $X$ shifted by one, as sets: $(X^1)_m = X_{m+1}$. The example: there is an M-polyfold all of whose points are smooth ($X_0 = X_\infty$) for which $1_0^1 : X \to X^1$ is not sc-smooth, so $X^1 \ne X$ as M-polyfolds. It is a retract $O \subseteq \mathbb R \oplus X$, $X$ the weighted sequence space of V1.13 ($|x|_m = \sup_k (k+1)^m|x_k|$), with a single chart: the image of $r(t, z) = (t, L(t)z)$, $L(t)$ the projection onto $\cos\theta\,e_{n_k} + \sin\theta\,e_{n_{k+1}}$ ($n_k = 2^k$), the angle $\theta$ turning from $0$ to $\pi/2$ with flat ends while $t$ runs through $[1/(k+2), 1/(k+1)]$, and $L(t) = 0$ for $t \le 0$. Its points are smooth, and the lift $O \to E_1$ is discontinuous at $0$, so $O$ is not an sc⁺-retract (Proposition 4.8). The sc-smoothness of $r$ comes from a criterion proved for it: for level operators $L(p)_m : Z_m \to W_m$ depending on a finite-dimensional parameter $p$, compatible with the inclusions, with $(p, z) \mapsto L(p)_mz$ continuous and $p \mapsto L(p)_m$ of class $C^\infty$ as a map into the operators $Z_{m+1} \to W_m$ (one level of loss), $(p, z) \mapsto L(p)z$ is sc-smooth. Book: Remark 4.3, p. 148. Hidden hypotheses: $1_0^1$ is defined on $X_1$ (the text: when $X_0 = X_\infty$). Deviation (stronger): the sc-diffeomorphism clause needs only $X = X_1$, not $X_0 = X_\infty$; "$X^1 \ne X$ is possible" has an example, which the text does not give, and in it $X$ and $X^1$ even have different topologies on the same set. "$X^1 \ne X$" is read as "$1_0^1$ is not sc-smooth", equivalently "the identity is not an sc-diffeomorphism". An example needs a retraction that loses a level in its first derivative, as the splicings of HWZ do (a retraction with $C^1$ level maps gives none: an argument, not formalized), so its sc-smoothness does not follow from Proposition 1.19. "$(X^1)_m = X_{m+1} = X_i$" misprints $X_0$; the topologies of the iterated levels are gap G.6 (Findings, items 5, 125, 140–146). Formerly "narrower", for the missing example (gap G.31, now closed).

HWZ §4.3, Theorem 4.23, p. 165 (proof pp. 165–166)

Let $A \subseteq Z$ be a smooth submanifold with tame induced structure and compact closure, $p = P|_A$, $\varepsilon > 0$ with (1) $p^{-1}(\lambda)$ compact and non-empty for $|\lambda| \le \varepsilon$, (2) "for $z \in A$ there exists a sc-complement $T_zA$ in $T_zZ$ contained in $T^R_zZ$". Verified edition V4.54

Let $X$ be tame and $A$ a smooth finite-dimensional submanifold of $\mathbb R^m \times X$ with tame induced structure and compact closure, $\varepsilon > 0$, and suppose (1) for $|\lambda| \le \varepsilon$ ($|\lambda|^2 = \sum\lambda_i^2$) the set $A \cap \{z_1 = \lambda\}$ is compact and non-empty, (2) $A$ is in general position at every point. Then there is $\Sigma \subseteq \{|\lambda| < \varepsilon\}$ whose complement in $\{|\lambda| < \varepsilon\}$ is Lebesgue-null, consisting of stratified regular values, such that for $\lambda \in \Sigma$ the fibre $A_\lambda$ is compact, a smooth finite-dimensional submanifold of $X$, in general position at each of its points, and its induced structure has a corner structure and is tame. With ordinary regular values the conclusion fails at the value: in $\mathbb R \times [0, \infty)$, $A = \{(x, x) : 0 \le x < 1\} \cup (-1, 1) \times \{5\}$ satisfies the hypotheses, $Dp$ is onto everywhere, and $A_0 = \{0, 5\}$ meets $\partial X$ (Findings, item 102).

to confirm$P^1 : Y_{1,1} \to X^1$ with the index raises of the strong bundle charts is a strong bundle, and for every sc-Fredholm section $f$, $f^1$ is an sc-Fredholm section of it, the filler condition on level $1$ included.

HWZ §5.2, Corollary 5.8, p. 173

Verified edition V5.14

The shifted strong bundle. $P^1 : Y^1 \to X^1$ is a strong bundle over the M-polyfold $X^1$ (Definition 2.51): its total space is $Y_{1,1}$, the level $1$ of the M-polyfold $Y[0]$ with its level topology; $P^1$ is the restriction of $P$; the fibre over $x$ is $P^{-1}(x) \cap Y_{1,1}$, a linear subspace, carrying the topology of $F_1$; and the atlas consists of the index raises $\Phi^1$ of the strong bundle charts $\Phi$ of $P$ (base chart the level chart $\varphi^1$, fibre model $F^1$, retraction $R$ restricted to $U^1 \triangleleft F^1$), compatible charts having compatible index raises. Its double levels are $(Y^1)_{m,k} = Y_{m+1,k+1}$. $f^1$ is sc-Fredholm. For every sc-Fredholm section $f$ (no compactness needed), $f^1 = f|_{X_1}$ is an sc-Fredholm section of $P^1$: it is sc-smooth, regularizing, and at every smooth point of $X^1$ it has the data of Definition 3.11 in the index raise $\Phi^1$ of the chart $\Phi$ of a datum $(g, s)$ of $f$ there. The principal part of $f^1$ is the level-$1$ map of that of $f$; $g^1$ is a filling germ of it, including condition (3) of Definition 3.4 on level $1$, which comes from a regularity statement at the centre of every datum of Definition 3.11: $v \in \ker Dr(0)$ and $Dk(0)v \in F_m$ imply $v \in E_m$, $k$ the fill defect. In a chart. The level shift $f^1$ of a basic germ $f$ on $\tilde C \oplus W$, $\tilde C$ a partial quadrant, is a basic germ on $\tilde C \oplus W^1$ with $B^1$ in place of $B$; if a principal part $k$ is conjugated to a basic germ $h$ by $\Psi$, then $k^1$ is conjugated to $h^1$ by the index raise $\Psi^1$. Hence for an sc-Fredholm section with compact solution set: the zeros in $X_1$ form a compact subset of $X_1$, and at every smooth point $x$, in the chart $\Phi$ centred at $x$ of the germ $(f, x)$ with filling germ $g$ and sc⁺-germ $s$ (the text's germ reading of Definition 3.11), the level-$1$ germ $(g - s)^1$ is conjugated to a basic germ (by the germ form of the index raise, which uses $g - s$ only near $0$) and $s^1$ is an sc⁺-germ on the shifted germ of $s$. Book: Corollary 5.8, p. 173 ("it is a priori clear that $f^i$ is sc-Fredholm", as a section of $P^i : Y^i \to X^i$). Hidden hypotheses: the bundle $Y^1 \to X^1$, which the text does not define ($Y[i]$ is defined for $i = 0, 1$ only): $Y^1 = Y_{1,1}$, the convention of $E^1$, forced by "$f^i$ is obtained by raising the index" (an sc-smooth section maps $X_1$ into $Y_{1,1}$, in general not into $Y_{1,2}$); $\tilde C$ a partial quadrant. Deviation: none; "it is a priori clear" hides condition (3) of the filling on level $1$, which does not follow from level $0$ alone (an sc-operator can be bijective on level $0$ and not onto on level $1$); it is proved for the data of Definition 3.11 by reducing to $g(0) = 0$ with Lemma 3.17 (subtracting the section $z \mapsto \Gamma(z, -g(0))$, which leaves the fill defect unchanged) and applying Proposition 3.52 in sc form. No hypothesis beyond the text's is added; tameness is not used, and the tame form (germ data in tame charts of $P^1$) is not stated (Findings, items 22, 140–146). Formerly "narrower": the bundle was not built and the filler on level $1$ not verified (gap G.41, now closed for each fixed $i$). In the text's germ reading of Definition 3.11 (phase 2; Findings, Chapter 3, item 333) $s^1$ is an sc⁺-germ on the shifted germ; in the whole-chart reading it was sc⁺ on all of $U^1$.

Definition 5.9: for every $x$ and open $U(x)$ an sc-smooth $f : X \to \mathbb R$ with $f \ne 0$ and $\operatorname{supp}(f) \subseteq U(x)$. Definition 5.29: $f$ "not identically zero".

Verified edition V5.16

$X$ admits sc-smooth bump functions if for every $x$ and every open $U \ni x$ there is an sc-smooth $f : X \to \mathbb R$ with $f(x) \ne 0$ and $\operatorname{supp} f \subseteq U$. Definition 5.29 as written ("$f$ not identically zero") is a separate notion, implied by the first. A point $x$ is a bump point if every open $U \ni x$ carries an sc-smooth $f$ with $f(x) \ne 0$ and $\operatorname{supp} f \subseteq U$: the first notion says that every point is a bump point, and the second follows if the bump points are dense. On an sc-Banach space $E$ (as an M-polyfold with the identity chart) the second notion makes every smooth point a bump point; on M-polyfolds built on sc-Hilbert spaces the first notion holds. Book: Definition 5.9, p. 173; Definition 5.29, p. 192. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): "$f \ne 0$" is read as $f(x) \ne 0$, the reading Proposition 5.30's proof uses. Whether the weak reading implies it is open only at non-smooth points: at a smooth point of an sc-Banach space a bump that is non-zero near $x$ is translated to $x$ by a smooth vector, and translation by a non-smooth vector does not preserve the levels; that the weak reading is exactly the density of the bump points is argued, one direction formalized (Findings, items 41, 160–163).

HWZ §5.3, p. 174

$\Gamma^{+,1}_U(P)$: the $s \in \Gamma^+(P)$ with $\operatorname{supp}(s) \subseteq U$ and $N(s(x)) \le 1$ for all $x$, a metric space for $\rho(s, s') = \sup_xN(s(x) - s'(x))$, not complete.

Verified edition V5.21

For an auxiliary norm $N$ and an open $U$, $\Gamma^{+,1}_U(P)$ is the set of sc⁺-sections $s$ with $\operatorname{supp} s \subseteq U$ and $N(s(x)) \le 1$ for all $x$ (the allowable sections). For two sc⁺-sections $N(s(x) - s'(x))$ is the norm of the difference in the fibre $(Y_{0,1})_x$. The uniform distance $\rho(s, s') = \sup_xN(s(x) - s'(x))$ is finite ($\rho \le 2$) and, for an auxiliary norm, a metric on $\Gamma^{+,1}_U(P)$; $\rho(s, s') \le \varepsilon$ iff $N(s(x) - s'(x)) \le \varepsilon$ for all $x$. For the trivial bundle $\mathbb R \times \mathbb R \to \mathbb R$ with $N(x, v) = |v|$ and $U = \mathbb R$ the metric space is not complete; for $U = \emptyset$ (any bundle) and over a point with fibre $\mathbb R^k$ (any $U$) it is complete. Book: §5.3, p. 174 ("a metric space ... not complete"). Hidden hypotheses: none for the metric. Deviation (restated): the text's "not complete" is false without a hypothesis (the cases $U = \emptyset$ and a point base) and is read as "not complete in general", proved by the example: $s_j(x) = (x, \sqrt{x^2 + 1/(j+1)^2}/(2\sqrt{1 + x^2}))$ is a $\rho$-Cauchy sequence of allowable sections whose pointwise limit has the fibre part $|x|/(2\sqrt{1 + x^2})$, not differentiable at $0$, while the fibre part of an sc⁺-section of the trivial bundle is $C^1$. Non-completeness in the text's setting ($U$ containing a non-isolated point over which $Y_{0,1} \ne 0$) is expected by the same mechanism and not formalized (Findings, items 47, 150–153).

HWZ §6.1, Definition 6.1, p. 201 (with pp. 200–201, 219)

For an sc-Fredholm section $f$ and a smooth point $x$, $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x) = \{(f - s)'(x) + a \mid a : T_xX \to Y_x$ an sc⁺-operator$\}$, where $s$ is a local sc⁺-section with $s(x) = f(x)$, made in a strong bundle chart as $s(y) = R(y, f(x))$. Its members differ by sc⁺-operators and are sc-Fredholm of one index $\mathrm{ind}(f, x)$; §6.5 adds that $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ is convex (p. 219).

Verified edition V6.1

At a chart point $p = (c, z)$ of a smooth point $x$, $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ is the set of operators $(f + s)'(x) + a : T_zO \to K_z$ for an sc⁺-section $s$ with $(f + s)(x) = 0$ and an sc⁺-operator $a$; for one such $s$ it is $(f + s)'(x)$ plus the sc⁺-operators. Two such sections give linearizations that differ by an sc⁺-operator; the members of $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ are Fredholm on level $0$, all of the index $\mathrm{ind}(f, x)$ of V3.98; $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ is convex, and it is not empty when $P$ has sc⁺-sections through the smooth points of its fibres, which bump functions give. Book: §6.1, pp. 200–201 (the sections $s$ and the paragraph before the definition), Definition 6.1, p. 201, and p. 219 (convexity); the index and Proposition 6.2 are V3.98. Hidden hypotheses: an sc⁺-section through $f(x)$; the text constructs a local one in a chart, the project uses global ones (HasScPlusSectionsThrough), which exist under the standing bump functions. Deviation (restated): made in a chart point; global sections; "sc-Fredholm" is proved on level $0$, which is what the determinant lines use, and not on every level (gap G.64). The paragraph before the definition compares $(f - s)'(x)$ with itself where $(f - t)'(x)$ is meant (possible misprint) (Findings, items 40, 41).

HWZ §6.2, pp. 203–204

$\lambda(E) = \Lambda^{\max}E$ and $\lambda^(E) = (\lambda(E))^$. For $\Phi : E \to F$ between spaces of the same dimension, $\lambda(\Phi)(a_1 \wedge \dots \wedge a_n) = \Phi(a_1) \wedge \dots \wedge \Phi(a_n)$, nontrivial iff $\Phi$ is an isomorphism, with $\lambda(\Psi \circ \Phi) = \lambda(\Psi) \circ \lambda(\Phi)$; $\lambda^(\Phi)$ is the dual of $\lambda(\Phi)$. The dual vector $v^$ of $v \ne 0$ in a line is fixed by $v^*(v) = 1$ (p. 204).

Verified edition V6.2

$\lambda(E)$ is the top exterior power of a finite-dimensional real space and $\lambda^(E)$ its dual, both lines; a change of basis multiplies the wedge by the determinant, also in one block of a two-block wedge, and adding to one block vectors of the span of the other does not change the wedge. For $v \ne 0$ in a line, $v^$ is the functional with $v^(v) = 1$. For $\dim E = \dim F$, $\lambda(\Phi)(a_1 \wedge \dots \wedge a_n) = \Phi a_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \Phi a_n$, with $\lambda(\Psi\Phi) = \lambda(\Psi)\lambda(\Phi)$, nonzero iff $\Phi$ is bijective; $\lambda^(\Phi)$ is its dual. Book: §6.2, pp. 203–204. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation: none.

HWZ §6.5, Theorem 6.41 and its proof, p. 229; the paragraph after it, pp. 229–230

Over a tame $X$, for a proper sc-Fredholm section $f$ with $(f, x)$ in general position to $\partial X$ at every zero and an orientation $o^f$ of $f$, the solution set $S = f^{-1}(0)$ is a smooth compact manifold with boundary with corners with a natural orientation. Proof: $T_xS = \ker f'(x)$ is oriented by $o^f_x$ since $f'(x)$ is onto, and the local prolongation of this orientation on $S$ is the Fredholm one. For $f$ not generic, a small perturbation $s$ supported near the zero set orients $S_{f+s}$.

Verified edition V6.61

Over a tame $X$, for a proper sc-Fredholm section $f$ with tame germ data in general position (Definition 5.17) at every zero, the solution set $S$ is compact, a smooth submanifold in general position with the induced structure of a tame manifold with boundary with corners (the conclusions of Theorem 5.18), and $T_xS = \ker f'(x)$, read in a chart. At a zero, $f'(x)$ lies in $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ and is onto, so an element $o_x$ of $\mathrm{Or}^f_x$ gives a ray of $\det f'(x) \cong \lambda(\ker f'(x)) = \lambda(T_xS)$, the tangent orientation. For an orientation $o$ of $f$ (Definition 6.40) and every sc-smooth path $\gamma$ of zeros in an orientable neighbourhood $V \subseteq U$, the kernels $\ker f'(\gamma_q)$ form a continuous family of subspaces, and the tangent orientations of $o$ form an orientation of its line bundle. The Fredholm side is the push-forward for the datum $S = 0$, $k = 0$, which along a path of zeros is the continuation between tangent orientations. Book: Theorem 6.41 and its proof, p. 229; the paragraph after it on $S_{f+s}$, pp. 229–230. Deviation (narrower): "a natural orientation" is read as the tangent orientations with their continuity along the sc-smooth paths of zeros in a chart, and "the local prolongation of the orientation on $S$ is the Fredholm one" as the identity of continuation and push-forward along such paths. HWZ §6.5, Remark 6.42, p. 230

For an oriented $(f, o)$ and an sc⁺-section $s$ of $Y \to X \times [0, 1]$, $\hat f(x, t) = f(x) + s(x, t)$ has a natural orientation from $o$ and the standard orientation of $[0, 1]$: for $L = (f - t)'(x)$ oriented by $h = (a_1 \wedge \dots \wedge a_n) \otimes (b_1 \wedge \dots \wedge b_l)^$, the operator $\tilde L(a, b) = La$ on $T_{(x,t)}(X \times [0, 1])$ is oriented by $\tilde h = (a_1 \wedge \dots \wedge a_n \wedge e) \otimes (b_1 \wedge \dots \wedge b_l)^$, $e$ the standard orientation of $[0, 1]$, and $\tilde L$ lies in the linearization space of $\hat f$ at $(x, t)$.

Verified edition V6.62

For Fredholm $L$, $\tilde L = L \oplus 0 : E \times \mathbb R \to F$ is Fredholm with $\ker\tilde L = \ker L \times \mathbb R$ and $\operatorname{coker}\tilde L = \operatorname{coker} L$, and $h \mapsto \tilde h$, $(a_1 \wedge \dots \wedge a_n) \otimes d^* \mapsto ((a_1, 0) \wedge \dots \wedge (a_n, 0) \wedge e) \otimes d^$ with $e = (0, 1)$, is an isomorphism $\det(L) \cong \det(\tilde L)$; in local determinant charts its coordinate is $(-1)^{\dim F/R(P) + \dim\operatorname{coker}L}$ times a continuous nowhere-zero function, and $(-1)^{\dim\operatorname{coker}L}\,h \mapsto \tilde h$ pulls continuous orientations back along $L \mapsto \tilde L$. In charts: for an sc-Fredholm $f$, an sc⁺-section $S$ of $\pi^*P \to \mathbb R \times X$, $\hat f = \tilde f + S$ with $\tilde f(t, y) = f(y)$, and the product chart point $(t, z)$, the operator $\hat L(\sigma, v) = Lv$ lies in $\mathrm{Lin}(\hat f, (t, x))$ for every $L \in \mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$, and an orientation $o$ of $\mathrm{DET}(f, x)$ gives exactly one orientation $\hat o$ of $\mathrm{DET}(\hat f, (t, x))$ with $\hat o(\hat L)$ the image of $o(L)$ for every $L$; $o \mapsto \hat o$ is injective. *Book: Remark 6.42, p. 230. Hidden hypotheses: $x$ smooth and $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ nonempty (implied by bump functions, V6.1); only the orientation of $\mathrm{DET}(f, x)$ at the one point is used. Deviation (narrower): at a point. As we read it, the literal $h \mapsto \tilde h$ is not continuous in $L$ where the parity of $\dim\operatorname{coker}L$ changes, so the orientation of $\mathrm{DET}(\hat f, (t, x))$ it defines could depend on the choice of $L$; the sign $(-1)^{\dim\operatorname{coker}L}$ (the sign of V6.40) is used, which agrees with the text's map when $L$ is onto. $X \times [0, 1]$ is read as $\mathbb R \times X$ (decision D2), with the parameter first, so $\tilde L(a, b) = La$ is conjugated by the swap of the factors. That $(t, y) \mapsto \hat o$ is an orientation of $\hat f$ in the sense of Definition 6.40, built from an orientation of $f$, is not formalized (gap G.66) (Findings, items 95–97).

Definition 7.1, groupoids and the orbit space

restated

to confirmA groupoid is a structure of maps with the laws on composable pairs, and $|X|$ is its orbit space with $\pi$.

laws on composable pairs onlycomposition total, junk elsewherebridge to Mathlib’s Groupoid
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §7.1, Definition 7.1 and the paragraph after it, pp. 225–226

A groupoid $X = (X, \mathbf X)$ is a small category consisting of the set $X$ of objects, denoted by $x$, and the set $\mathbf X$ of morphisms (arrows), which are assumed to be invertible, and the following five structure maps $(s, t, m, u, \iota)$. (1) The source and target maps $s, t : \mathbf X \to X$ assign to every morphism $\varphi : x \to y$ in $\mathbf X$ its source $s(\varphi) = x$ and its target $t(\varphi) = y$. (2) The associative multiplication (composition) map $m : \mathbf X\,{}_s{\times}_t\,\mathbf X \to \mathbf X$, $m(\varphi, \psi) = \varphi \circ \psi$, is defined on the fibered product $\mathbf X\,{}_s{\times}_t\,\mathbf X = \{(\varphi, \psi) \in \mathbf X \times \mathbf X \mid s(\varphi) = t(\psi)\}$, so that if $\psi : x \to z$ and $\varphi : z \to y$, then $\varphi \circ \psi : x \to y$. (3) For every object $x \in X$ there exists the unit morphism $1_x : x \to x$ in $\mathbf X$, a 2-sided unit for the composition: $\varphi \circ 1_x = \varphi$ and $1_x \circ \psi = \psi$ for all $\varphi, \psi \in \mathbf X$ satisfying $s(\varphi) = x = t(\psi)$; these define the unit map $u : X \to \mathbf X$, $u(x) = 1_x$. (4) For every morphism $\varphi : x \to y$ there exists the inverse morphism $\varphi^{-1} : y \to x$, a 2-sided inverse: $\varphi \circ \varphi^{-1} = 1_y$ and $\varphi^{-1} \circ \varphi = 1_x$; these define the inverse map $\iota : \mathbf X \to \mathbf X$, $\iota(\varphi) = \varphi^{-1}$.

After the definition: $\mathrm{mor}(x, y) \subset \mathbf X$ is the set of all morphisms $\varphi$ with $s(\varphi) = x$ and $t(\varphi) = y$. The orbit space $|X| = X/\sim$ is the quotient of the set of objects by the equivalence relation $x \sim y$ if and only if there exists a morphism $\varphi : x \to y$; the class of $x$ is $|x| := \{y \in X \mid y \sim x\}$, and $\pi : X \to |X|$, $\pi(x) = |x|$, is the quotient map.

Verified edition V7.1

A groupoid is a set of objects and a set of invertible morphisms with source, target, an associative composition on composable pairs, units and inverses; $|X|$ is the quotient by $x \sim y$ iff there is a morphism $x \to y$, with projection $\pi$. Book: Definition 7.1 and the paragraph after it, pp. 225–226. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): a structure of maps on types, the laws required on composable pairs and the composition total with a junk value; the saturation $\pi^{-1}(\pi(A))$ of Definition 7.10 is defined here; the bridge to Mathlib's CategoryTheory.Groupoid is added so that "full" and "faithful" are Mathlib's (Findings, item 1).

HWZ §7.1, Definition 7.3, pp. 226–227

An ep-groupoid $X = (X, \mathbf X)$ consists of a groupoid equipped with M-polyfold structures on the object set $X$ and the morphism set $\mathbf X$ having the following properties. (1) (étale) The source and target maps $s, t : \mathbf X \to X$ are local sc-diffeomorphisms. (2) The unit map $u$ and the inverse map $\iota$ are sc-smooth. (3) (Properness) Every point $x \in X$ possesses an open neighborhood $V(x)$ of $x$ in $X$ such that the map $t : s^{-1}(\mathrm{cl}_X(V(x))) \to X$ is proper. Since $s$ is a local sc-diffeomorphism, the fibered product $\mathbf X\,{}_s{\times}_t\,\mathbf X$ is in a natural way an M-polyfold in view of Lemma 2.8 in [38], and we require (4) the multiplication map $m : \mathbf X\,{}_s{\times}_t\,\mathbf X \to \mathbf X$ is sc-smooth. In particular, all the structure maps $(s, t, m, u, \iota)$ are sc-smooth maps.

Verified edition V7.3

An ep-groupoid is a groupoid with M-polyfold structures on objects and morphisms such that (1) $s, t$ are local sc-diffeomorphisms, (2) $u$ and $\iota$ are sc-smooth, (3) every $x$ has an open $V(x)$ with $t : s^{-1}(\mathrm{cl}_X V(x)) \to X$ proper, (4) $m$ is sc-smooth on the fibred product $\mathbf X\,{}_s{\times}_t\,\mathbf X$; all structure maps are then sc-smooth. Book: Definition 7.3, pp. 226–227. Hidden hypotheses: Obj and Mor Hausdorff and paracompact (the project's M-polyfolds). Deviation (restated): (3) existential per point, with Mathlib's proper maps; the universal form "for every open $V \ni x$" fails (the pair groupoid of $\mathbb Z$), and every smaller open neighbourhood works. (4) on the sub-M-polyfold of Part I's Proposition 2.15, the book's statement of the text's citation "Lemma 2.8 in [38]" (an external reference, not a misprint); the proofs use the equivalent sheet form (Findings, items 3, 4, 103).

HWZ §7.1, Definition 7.3 (3), p. 227; used on pp. 230–254

Definition 7.3 (3) asks that $t : s^{-1}(\mathrm{cl}_X(V(x))) \to X$ be proper. The proofs use this in the form: if $s(\varphi_k) \in \mathrm{cl}_X(V(x))$ and $t(\varphi_k)$ converges in $X$, then, "after perhaps taking a subsequence", $(\varphi_k)$ converges in $\mathbf X$ (Proposition 7.3, p. 230; Lemma 7.1, p. 230; Proposition 7.7, p. 238; Proposition 7.11, p. 248; Lemma 7.8, p. 254), or through the compactness of preimages of compact sets (Proposition 7.13, p. 251). After Definition 7.4 (p. 227) the text points out that this properness differs from that of classical Lie groupoids, which requires $(s, t) : \mathbf X \to X \times X$ to be proper, a requirement too weak for some of the constructions.

Verified edition V7.4

For the restriction of $t$ to a closed $s^{-1}(Q)$ between metrizable spaces, properness is equivalent to: every sequence with convergent targets has a convergent subsequence; it passes to smaller closures, and proper restrictions have closed images and finite fibres. Book: the notion of Definition 7.3 (3), p. 227, used in sequential form in Proposition 7.3, Lemma 7.1 (p. 230), Proposition 7.7 (p. 238), Proposition 7.11 (p. 248), Proposition 7.13 (p. 251) and Lemma 7.8 (p. 254). Hidden hypotheses: metrizability (Theorem 2.2), which M-polyfolds have. Deviation (not in the book): the equivalence is used without comment in the text (Findings, item 3).

HWZ §7.1, Definition 7.4 and the paragraph before it, p. 227

Since $s, t : \mathbf X \to X$ are local sc-diffeomorphisms, every morphism $\varphi : x \to y$ of an ep-groupoid has an extension to a local sc-diffeomorphism $\hat\varphi$ satisfying $\hat\varphi(x) = y$, defined as follows: there exist open neighborhoods $\mathbf U(\varphi) \subset \mathbf X$ and $U(x), U(y) \subset X$ such that $s : \mathbf U(\varphi) \to U(x)$ and $t : \mathbf U(\varphi) \to U(y)$ are sc-diffeomorphisms, and $\hat\varphi = t \circ (s|\mathbf U(\varphi))^{-1} : U(x) \to U(y)$. In the case that $\varphi$ is smooth, i.e. $\varphi \in \mathbf X_\infty$, there is an associated sc-isomorphism $T\varphi : T_{s(\varphi)}X \to T_{t(\varphi)}X$ defined by $T\varphi := T\hat\varphi(x)$; more generally $T\hat\varphi : TU(s(\varphi)) \to TU(t(\varphi))$. $T\varphi$ can be defined for $\varphi$ on level at least $1$ and gives a bounded linear isomorphism on level $0$; only in the case that $\varphi$ is smooth is $T\varphi$ an sc-operator. Definition 7.4: associated to a smooth morphism $\varphi$ we have the so-called associated local sc-diffeomorphism $\hat\varphi$, as well as its tangent $T\varphi$.

Verified edition V7.5

For a morphism $\varphi : x \to y$ there are open $\mathbf U(\varphi)$, $U(x)$, $U(y)$ with $s : \mathbf U(\varphi) \to U(x)$, $t : \mathbf U(\varphi) \to U(y)$ sc-diffeomorphisms, and $\hat\varphi = t \circ (s|\mathbf U(\varphi))^{-1} : U(x) \to U(y)$ is an sc-diffeomorphism with $\hat\varphi(x) = y$; $T\varphi := T\hat\varphi(x)$. Book: p. 227 (the paragraph before the definition) and Definition 7.4, p. 227. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (narrower): $\hat\varphi$ is verified; $T\varphi$ is a definition only, and that it is a bounded linear isomorphism on level $0$ for $\varphi \in \mathbf X_1$ and an sc-isomorphism for smooth $\varphi$ is not verified (gaps G.7, G.70). The display reads "$\hat\varphi = t \circ (s|\mathbf U(\varphi))^{-1} \circ U(x) \to U(y)$", $\circ$ for $:$ (possible misprint), and "$T\varphi : T_{s(\varphi)}X \to T_{t(\varphi)}$" lacks the $X$ (possible misprint or extraction artefact) (Findings, items 5, 110).

the levels of an ep-groupoid and the filtration of $|X|$

narrower

to confirm$s, t$ preserve levels and the degeneracy index, so $ml$ and $d_X$ are constant on classes.

$|X_\infty|$ not stated: gap G.72
the full statement, HWZ beside Lean

HWZ §7.1, pp. 227–228

The M-polyfolds $X$ and $\mathbf X$ are equipped with the filtrations $X = X_0 \supset X_1 \supset X_2 \supset \dots \supset X_\infty = \bigcap_{k \ge 0} X_k$ and similarly for $\mathbf X$; $X_\infty$ is dense in every $X_k$. For $x$ in the M-polyfold $X$, $ml(x) \in \mathbb N \cup \{\infty\}$ is the largest non-negative integer $m$, or $\infty$, such that $x \in X_m$. Since the source and target maps are local sc-diffeomorphisms and therefore preserve the levels, $ml(x) = ml(y) = ml(\varphi)$ for every morphism $\varphi : x \to y$; consequently the filtration of $X$ induces the filtration $|X| = |X_0| \supset |X_1| \supset \dots \supset |X_\infty| = \bigcap_{k \ge 0}|X_k|$ of the orbit space. The degeneracy indices $d_X : X \to \mathbb N$ and $d_{\mathbf X} : \mathbf X \to \mathbb N$ are invariant under local sc-diffeomorphisms (Proposition 2.7), so $d_X(s(\varphi)) = d_{\mathbf X}(\varphi) = d_X(t(\varphi))$ for every morphism $\varphi$; in particular $d_X(x) = d_X(x')$ if $x \sim x'$.

Verified edition V7.6

$s$ and $t$ preserve the levels, so $ml(x) = ml(\varphi) = ml(y)$ for $\varphi : x \to y$; $d_X(s(\varphi)) = d_{\mathbf X}(\varphi) = d_X(t(\varphi))$, so $d_X$ is constant on classes; $|X_k| = \pi(X_k)$. Book: pp. 227–228, with Part I's Proposition 2.7. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (narrower): the set $|X_\infty|$ and $|X_\infty| = \bigcap_k |X_k|$ are not stated (gap G.72); the density of $X_\infty$ is Part I's (Findings, items 6, 112).

HWZ §7.1, Definition 7.6 and the paragraph after it, p. 228

The ep-groupoid $(X, \mathbf X)$ is called tame if the object space $X$ is a tame M-polyfold as introduced in Definition 2.19. In a tame ep-groupoid not only $X$ is a tame M-polyfold but also $\mathbf X$ is a tame M-polyfold. This follows from the facts that $\mathbf X$ is locally sc-diffeomorphic by $s$ to $X$ and the tameness condition is invariant under local sc-diffeomorphisms.

Verified edition V7.8

$X$ is tame if the object M-polyfold is tame; then the morphism M-polyfold is tame. Book: Definition 7.6 and the paragraph after it, p. 228. HWZ §7.1, after Definition 7.7, pp. 228–229

It is sufficient to require that the functor $f$ is sc-smooth between the object spaces $X \to Y$, because the sc-smoothness of $f : \mathbf X \to \mathbf Y$ follows from the properties of the source map $s : \mathbf X \to X$: given $\varphi \in \mathbf X$ and $f(\varphi) = \psi \in \mathbf Y$ there exist open neighborhoods $\mathbf U(\varphi)$, $\mathbf U(\psi)$, $U(s(\varphi))$ and $U(s(\psi))$ satisfying $f(U(s(\varphi))) \subset U(s(\psi))$ and $f(\mathbf U(\varphi)) \subset \mathbf U(\psi)$; moreover, $s : \mathbf U(\varphi) \to U(s(\varphi))$ and $s : \mathbf U(\psi) \to U(s(\psi))$ are sc-diffeomorphisms. Therefore the claim follows from the formula $f(\gamma) = (s|\mathbf U(\psi))^{-1}(f(s(\gamma)))$ for all $\gamma \in \mathbf U(\varphi)$.

Verified edition V7.10

The text claims that a functor sc-smooth on objects is sc-smooth on morphisms, by $f(\gamma) = (s|\mathbf U(\psi))^{-1}(f(s(\gamma)))$ on $\mathbf U(\varphi)$. Book: pp. 228–229. Hidden hypotheses: the argument needs $f(\mathbf U(\varphi)) \subseteq \mathbf U(\psi)$, i.e. continuity of $f$ on morphisms. Deviation (does not hold as we read it): a functor of the trivial $\mathbb Z/3$-action on $\mathbb R$, the identity on objects, is sc-smooth on objects and not continuous on morphisms; for functors continuous on morphisms the claim is proved, with a sheet $\mathbf U(\psi)$ at $\psi = f(\varphi)$ and $\mathbf U(\varphi) = f^{-1}(\mathbf U(\psi))$ (Findings, items 9, 104).

HWZ §7.1, p. 232

The natural functor $\Gamma : G \ltimes U = (U, G \times U) \to (X, \mathbf X)$ maps, on object level, $y \in U$ to $y \in X$ and, on the morphism level, the morphism $(g, y) \in G \times U$ into the unique morphism $\Gamma(g, y) \in \mathbf X$. By property (3) of Theorem 7.1 the functor $\Gamma$ is full and faithful (fully faithful): for two objects $y$ and $z$ in $G \ltimes U$ it induces a surjection (full) and an injection (faithful) $\mathrm{mor}_{G \ltimes U}(y, z) \to \mathrm{mor}_X(y, z)$. The image of the functor $\Gamma$ is the full subcategory $(U(x), \mathbf U(x))$ of $(X, \mathbf X)$; hence $\Gamma$ identifies the translation groupoid $G_x \ltimes U(x)$ with the category $(U(x), \mathbf U(x))$.

HWZ §7.1, Proposition 7.5, pp. 233–234 (proof pp. 234–236)

Let $(X, \mathbf X)$ be an ep-groupoid and $Y = \{y_1, \dots, y_k\}$ a finite set of distinct objects in $X$ which are mutually isomorphic. Denote by $\mathbf Y = (Y, \mathbf Y)$ the full subcategory associated with $Y$, whose morphism set is $\mathbf Y$. Then, given a neighborhood $V$ of $Y$ in $X$, there exists a functor $f$, which associates with the objects $y$ in $Y$ mutually disjoint connected open neighborhoods $U(y)$ contained in $V$, and with a morphism $\psi : y \to y'$ in $\mathbf Y$ an sc-diffeomorphism $f(\psi) : U(y) \to U(y')$. The set of morphisms $\mathbf U = \{\varphi \in \mathbf X \mid s(\varphi) \text{ and } t(\varphi) \in \bigcup_{y \in Y}U(y)\}$ decomposes into the union of connected components $\mathbf U(\psi)$, $\psi \in \mathbf Y$, and the following holds true. (1) The isotropy group $G_y$ for $y \in Y$ acts via the natural action on $U(y)$. (2) For $\psi \in \mathbf Y$ the maps $s : \mathbf U(\psi) \to U(y)$ and $t : \mathbf U(\psi) \to U(y)$ are sc-diffeomorphisms. (3) If $\psi : y \to y'$ and $z \in U(y)$, then $f(\psi)(z) = t \circ (s|\mathbf U(\psi))^{-1}(z)$.

Verified edition V7.25

For finitely many mutually isomorphic objects $Y$ and a neighbourhood $V$ of $Y$ there is a functor $f$ assigning disjoint connected open $U(y) \subseteq V$ and sc-diffeomorphisms $f(\psi) : U(y) \to U(y')$, such that the morphisms between the $U(y)$ split into components $\mathbf U(\psi)$ with (1) the natural action of $G_y$ on $U(y)$, (2) $s, t : \mathbf U(\psi) \to U(y)$ sc-diffeomorphisms, (3) $f(\psi) = t \circ (s|\mathbf U(\psi))^{-1}$. Book: Proposition 7.5, pp. 233–236. Hidden hypotheses: none. Deviation (restated): proved by transporting one natural representation along chosen morphisms from a base object, without the text's induction or shrinking; $V$ a neighbourhood of the set $Y$; $Y = \emptyset$ allowed. Twelve possible misprints in the proof, one possibly an extraction artefact (Findings, items 25, 26).

HWZ §7.1, Proposition 7.6, p. 236 (proof pp. 236–237)

Let $X$ be an ep-groupoid and $z \in |X|$. We fix $x \in X$ satisfying $z = |x|$, denote the isotropy group of $x$ by $G_x$ and take an open neighborhood $U(x)$ of $x$ on which we have the natural $G_x$-action $\Phi$, which we abbreviate as $g \ast y := \Phi(g)(y)$ for $g \in G_x$ and $y \in U(x)$. Then the map $\tau : G_x\backslash U(x) \to |U(x)| = \pi(U(x))$, $G_x \ast y \mapsto |y|$, is a homeomorphism. In other words, the obvious functor $G_x \ltimes U(x) \to X$, which on the object level is the inclusion map and on the morphism level the map $(g, y) \mapsto \Gamma(g, y)$, is a fully faithful functor, which on the orbit spaces defines a homeomorphism between the orbit spaces $|U(x)|_{G_x \ltimes U(x)} = G_x\backslash U(x)$ and $|U(x)| = \pi(U(x))$.

HWZ §7.2, Definition 7.11 and the sentences after it, p. 239

An ep-groupoid $X$ is said to be effective provided for every $x \in X$ and $g \in G_x \setminus \{1_x\}$, given an open neighborhood $\mathbf U(g) \subset \mathbf X$, there exists a morphism $\psi \in \mathbf U(g)$ satisfying $s(\psi) \ne t(\psi)$. An object $x \in X$ is said to be regular provided $G_x = \{1_x\}$. If $\varphi \in \mathbf X$ and $s(\varphi)$ is a regular object, the same has to be true for $t(\varphi)$. The regular part $X_{reg}$ of an ep-groupoid is the subset $X_{reg} = \{x \in X \mid G_x = \{1_x\}\}$ of the object space $X$.

Every point $x$ of the object set possesses a suitable open neighborhood $U(x)$, which can be chosen arbitrarily small, on which $G_x$ acts by the homomorphism $\Phi : G_x \to \mathrm{Diff}_{sc}(U(x))$. We say that $g \in G_x$ acts trivially if there exists an open neighborhood $U(x)$ equipped with the $G_x$-action $\Phi : G_x \to \mathrm{Diff}_{sc}(U(x))$ such that $g$ belongs to the kernel of $\Phi$, i.e., $\Phi(g) = 1$. Clearly $1_x$ always acts trivially, but there might be other elements $g \in G_x$ acting trivially. Since $G_x$ is finite, we can choose $U(x)$ so small that the kernel of $\Phi$ is equal to the subgroup of $G_x$ acting trivially on $U(x)$. We denote by $T_x \subset G_x$ the subgroup of $G_x$ acting trivially on $U(x)$, which, as the kernel of a group homomorphism, is a normal subgroup of $G_x$.

HWZ §7.5.1, Theorem 7.5 and its proof, pp. 253–254

Given an ep-groupoid $X$, an object $x_0 \in X$, and an open neighborhood $V \subset X$ of $x_0$. Then there exist an open neighborhood $U \subset V$ of $x_0$, a group homomorphism $\Phi : G_{x_0} \to \mathrm{Diff}_{sc}(U)$, $g \mapsto \Phi(g) = t_g \circ s_g^{-1}$, and an sc-smooth map $\Gamma : G_{x_0} \times U \to \mathbf X$ having the following properties: $\Gamma(g, x_0) = g$; $s(\Gamma(g, y)) = y$ and $t(\Gamma(g, y)) = \Phi(g)(y)$ for all $y \in U$ and $g \in G_{x_0}$; if $h : y \to z$ is a morphism connecting two objects $y, z \in U$, then there exists a unique $g \in G_{x_0}$ such that $\Gamma(g, y) = h$. In particular, every morphism between points in $U$ belongs to the image of the map $\Gamma$. The homomorphism $\Phi$ is called a natural representation of the stabilizer group $G_{x_0}$. (In the proof, for every $g \in G_{x_0}$ one chooses contractible open neighborhoods $N^t_g$, $N^s_g$ on which $t$ and $s$ are sc-diffeomorphisms onto some open neighborhood $U_0$ of $x_0$, the sets $N^t_g \cup N^s_g$ disjoint; $N_g := N^t_g \cap N^s_g$, $s_g := s|N_g$, $t_g := t|N_g$, and $\Gamma(g, y) = s_g^{-1}(y)$.)

Verified edition V7.62

HWZ §7.5.2, proof of Theorem 7.4, pp. 255–256

Consider the open covering $(|U_\lambda|)_{\lambda \in \Lambda}$ of $|X|$. For every $x \in X$ take an open neighborhood $V(x)$ with: (1) there exists an open neighborhood $W(x)$ equipped with the natural $G_x$-action such that $V(x) \subset \mathrm{cl}_X(V(x)) \subset W(x)$ and $V(x)$ is invariant; (2) $t : s^{-1}(\mathrm{cl}_X(V(x))) \to X$ is proper; (3) there exists a $\lambda$ with $V(x) \subset U_\lambda$; (4) $(\pi^{-1}(|V(x)|) \setminus V(x)) \cap W(x) = \emptyset$. Take a locally finite refinement $(V'_i)_{i \in I}$ of $(|V(x)|)_{x \in X}$, with $V'_i \subset |V(x_i)|$, open $V''_i$ with $V''_i \subset \mathrm{cl}_{|X|}(V''_i) \subset V'_i$ and $|X| = \bigcup_i V''_i$; $U''_i = V(x_i) \cap \pi^{-1}(V''_i)$ is invariant under the $G_{x_i}$-action, with saturation $U_i = \pi^{-1}(V''_i)$. Take a continuous partition of unity $(\beta_i)$ subordinate to $(V''_i)$; $(\beta_i \circ \pi)|V(x_i)$ has support in $U''_i \subset V(x_i)$. Using the sc-smooth partitions of unity of $X$, approximate $(\beta_i \circ \pi)|V(x_i)$ by Lemma 7.10 by an sc-smooth $f_i$ supported in $V(x_i)$ with $f_i \ge (\beta_i \circ \pi)|V(x_i)$; average using the $G_{x_i}$-action, extend to the saturation of $V(x_i)$ and then by $0$ outside, which gives a function $h_i$ compatible with morphisms. The sum $h$ of all $h_i$ is locally finite and always bigger than $0$, and $(h_i/h)$ is the desired partition of unity for the ep-groupoid $X$.
